The Peace Conferences were duly opened at Paris on Monday last ; and the prayers of all good men are with the negotiators for a happy and honourable issue to their labours. As yet, however, all is conjecture as to the points upon which they may agree or disagree, and indeed as to the instructions they have received from their respective governments which will guide their conduct. In the absence of real information, the correspondents of the daily þÿpress who must make up their column, if the force of verbiage can so far þÿgo have been indulging in vague speculations as to what may be and what may not he the case elaborate disquisitions upon the external appearance of the official residence of the Minister of Foreign Affairs at þÿParis the moral and physical condition of the officials, doorkeepers, and other employes about that department, under existing circumstances of exciting interþÿest and a variety of small topics calculated to gratify a morbid vulgar curiosity. A sample of this trash we reproduce in another column, from the letters of þÿ our own þÿcorrespondent þÿof the leading þÿjournal; upon whose authority also, we quote the following remarkable revelations : þÿ The sittings of the Congress will not take place consecutively day after day. In some few cases it may he so, hut such is not the present intention. The number of times in the week that the plenipotentiaries will meet for despatch ol business is not fixed ; it may he three or four times, or oftener, and

three days or more may elapse between two sittings; but this will depend a good deal on þÿcircumstances. This must he authentic; it must be accepted as certain that " the number ot times in the week that the þÿ plenipoþÿ business is not fixed þÿ; tentiaries will meet for despatch of it may, indeed, be three or tour times, or even oftener, þÿ the writer does not venture so far as to assert it may he less; hut in this lie speaks ex cathedra, and with an exactitude that may defy the most rigorous scrutiny : that supposing the meetings to take place three or four times a week, þÿ three days or more may elapse between two þÿsittings, in which case, though this ingenious writer does not think it necessary to insist on the fact, the remaining meetings in the week will of necessity take place "consecutively from day to þÿday. In the midst of all this small talk it is important to know that the negotiators have agreed to an Armistice, not to interfere with any blockades now established or to he established, and limited in duration to the 31st of March, from which we are to infer that by the 1st of April matters will he definitively arj ranged one way or the other. For the ultimate result, to judge from rumours which reach us on every side, we should he inclined to hope for the best þÿ for Peace and all its countless blessings. One very material point, which once was said to threaten disagreement, namely the including of Nicolaieffin the clause enforcing the neutral character of the Black Sea, has

been, it is said, consented to in the sense fixed by the Allies. Another no less important, þÿ that relating to the dismantling of Bomarsund and the Aland Islands, has also, it is said, been conceded.
For the general bearings of the negotiations the public cannot expect to be fullv informed for another week or ten days at the least.

From the London Weekly Dispatch. SWEDEN. The Swedish diplomatist, Lallenstaedt, is about to publish a pamphlet. According to this authority, both the King and the Crown Prince Charles were, from the very beginning of the Oriental complication of affairs, of the necessity ot making perfectly alliance an aware with the Western Powers, although such a step must naturally be only taken with the greatest caution. The offer of the Aland Islands was rejected by Sweden, after the capture and destruction of Bomarsund, because they were considered untenable without the possession of Finland. The treaty of the 2nd of December, 1854, led King Oscar to believe that Austria was going to take an active part in the war. In the month of March last year the negotiations were opened at Paris. King Oscar demanded pecuniary subsidies and an army of a hundred thousand men, to lie supported by 60,000 Swedes. It they succeeded in conquering Finland, it was to be given again to Sweden. In the meantime the Allies decided on confining the operations for the year 1855 to the Crimea, with merely a demonstration in the Baltic. The real bona-fide Baltic campaign was adjourned, and it was only after the fall of Sebastopol that the negotiations with Sweden were renewed by the memorable mission of General Canrobert to Stockholm, and there is every reason to believe that if the Conferences at Paris are broken off, and hostilities re-comnience, Sweden will boldly throw off her neutrality, and take an active and honourable part in the campaign, for which every prepara-
tion has been making for a long time, both as regards the navy, the land forces, and the artillery.

Just as we were preparing for Press we have received files of Demerara Royal Gazette, of the 1st instant, we find that the late riots had been suppressed, ar.d that the Courts were busy examining and condemning the offenders according to the degrees of the offence. Several war vessels had arrived in the river as well as detachments of troops from Barbados. Two men, Aluey.x and Culdeparan, had been executed at noon that day. The paper says : þÿ þÿ has It been suggested that the late riotous conduct of our free negroes will exercise a prejudicial effect upon the general cause of emancipation. No doubt it will be so made use of, though it is a poor argument for slavery, indeed no argument at all. But the probability of its being so used in one reason why all good men must lament these occurrences. þÿ With regard to the convicted offenders, we are glad to observe that the Government are disposed to be lenient, and indeed the obvious policy in all such cases is, to punish severely the ringleaders and instigators, and deal leniently with the ignorant multitude

Any thing like general severe punishment is to be avoided, inasmuch as it would only bye and bye send abroad into the community a multitude of disaffected criminals. The atmosphere of a gaol ora penal settlement is morally bad, and we are glad, therefore, that many of the minor offenders have been dismissed with no other punishment than a compulsory industry. This will surely convince them that the Government has no desire to punish and no object in view but their own substantial þÿgood.

Engagements. þÿ The thoughtlessness of youth and the headlong impetus of passion frequently throw people into rash engagements, and in these cases the formal morality of the world, more careful of externals than of truth, declares it to be nobler for such rash engagements to be kept, even when the rashness is felt by the engaged, than that a þÿman h s onour should be stained by a withdrawal. The letter thus takes precedence of the spirit. To satisfy this prejudice a life is sacrificed. A miserable marriage rescues the honor ; and no one throws the burden of that misery upon the prejudice. I am not forgetting the necessity of being stringent against the common thoughtlessness of youth in forming such relations ; but I say that this thoughtlessness once having occurred, reprobate it as you will, the pain which a separation may bring had better be endured than evaded by an unholy marriage, which cannot come to good.

Naturae Characteristics. þÿ A Frenchman, an Englishman, and a German, were commissioned, it is said, to give the world the benefit of their views on that interesting animal, the camel Away goes the Frenchman to the Jardm des Plantes , spends an hour there in rapid investigation, returns, and writes a feuilleton, in which there is no phrase the Academy can blame, but also no phrase which can add to the general knowledge. He is perfectly satisfied, however, and says, le voilo , It thameau ! The Englishman packs up his tea-caddy, and a magazine of comforts ; pitches his tent in the East ; remains there two years studying the camel in its habits ; and returns with a thick volume of facts, arranged without order, expounded without philosophy, but serving for valuable meterials for all who come after him. The German, despising the frivolity of the Frenchman, and the unpbiloeophic matter-of-factness of the Englishman, retires to his study, there to tonstruct the idea of a camel out of the depths of his moral consciousness þÿ and he is still at it.

Dr. Rush tells us that when he was called upon to attend, on their deathbeds, aged Swedes, who for forty, fifty, and sixty years had lost the use of their native tongue, the long suspended faculty would be recalled in approaching death, and they would talk, pray, and sing in Swedish. Dr. Johnson, also, when it came to his turn to die, spoke not in the march of his own majestic rhetoric þÿ passed by even the cadences of those Latin hymns in which he had so much loved to dwell þÿ but was heard with his sinking voice muttering a þÿchild s rian. prayer which he had learned on his moþÿther s knee. The case had attracted the particular attention of a young physician, and by his statement many eminent physiologists and psychologists visited the town, and examined the case on the spot. Sheets full of her ravings were taken down from her mouth, and were found to consist of sentences coherent and intelligible each for itself, but with little or no connection with

each other. All trick or conspiracy was out of the question. Not only had the young woman ever been a harmless, simple creature, but she was evidently laboring with nervous fever. The Man who never Laughs þÿ In a sermon delivered by the Rev. Dr. Bellows, of New York, before the Western Unitarian Conference, is the following paragraph : þÿ For my own part, I say it in all solemnity, I have lived to become sincerely suspicious of the piety of those

who do not love pleasure in any form. I cannot trust the man that never laughs ; that is always sedate ; that has no apparent outlet for those natural springs of sportiveness and gaiety that are perennial in the human soul. I know that nature takes her revenge on such violence. 1 expect to find secret vices, malignant sins, or horrid crimes springing up in this hot-bed of confined air and imprisoned space ; and therefore it gives me a sincere moral gratification anywhere, and in any community, to see innocent pleasure and popular amusement resisting the religious bigotry that frowns so unwisely upon them. Anything is better than the dark, dead, unhappy social life þÿ a prey to annual and morbid excitement, which results from unmittigated puritanism, whose second crop is usually unbridled license and infamous folly.

FATAL ACCIDENT. The only local incident that has come to our knowledge since last issue is one of a truly painful character ; and in chronicling the melancholy circumstance we deeply sympathize with the surviving relatives on the fatal occurrence. From all lhe information that we have collected, it appears that on Wednesday afternoon last Mr. George Boron, shoemaker, of this town, visited the estate " Granard," the property of J. W. Hope, Esqr., for the purpose of attending a funeral there þÿ but inasmuch as the procession was not ready to move on his arrival, he took a walk around the plantation, and while in the boiling-house in conversation with two other persons he suddenly turned þÿ whether from an attack of vertigo, or a slip none can say þÿ and fell into one of the coppers containing the raw liquor; lie was immediately removed by the parties present, and although life was not extinct, it was perceptible that he could not survive. Medical aid was called in, and every atten- I tion was afforded by the proprietor of the property, yet he did not live for many j hours after. His remains were brought into town yesterday morning, and interred in the afternoon. By this untoward event j an affectionate wife and several children have been plunged into the sorest afflicj tion.

DENMARK. þÿ Ilis Majesty the King had opened the session of the Supremo Council of the Kingdom with unusual pomp, accompanied by the Hereditary Prince and the whole Court. In the Speech, the King stated his satisfaction at seeing around him representatives of all parties in the monarchy. He expressed the hope that the assemblage would have the effect of rendering more close and firm the bonds that united them all, and that their union would be a safeguard against dangers from without, and at the same time insure the development- of internal progress. Thanking God for the past maintenance of peace, His Majesty concluded with a prayer that Providence might further remove all menacing contingencies. The Ministers brought forward no Bills, as nothing important will be submitted to Hi unci' during the present meting, t ;vh is to be immediately followed by an ordinary session. FRANCE. -The Legislative session was opened on Mi n ;'ie 3rd March, by the Emperor in p Tuileries, in the Salle del Marechaux, V .,h a Speech, which will be found annexed. The Speech was rec< red < nthuiiaatie applause ; and Z - ror was most enthusiastically ri e-ived i : i his passage to and from the Salle des Marechaux ; but the language of the Speech was considered much cooler in regard to the prospect of peace than was anticipated, and a certain degree of disapprobation was manifested

throughout Paris that more had not been said regarding the state of the negotiations. The Emperor said : þÿ MM. les Pairs. MM. les Senateubs, þÿ The last time that I summoned you to meet, grave anxieties weighed upon us. The Allied armies were exhausting themselves in a seige, ir. which the stubbornness of the defenders made success doubtful. Europe, uncertain, seemed to await the issue of the struggle before declaring herself. To sustain the war, I asked a loan, which, although it might appear excessive, you voted unanimously, The high price of provisions me naced the labouring classes with general disc>>mfort, and a disturbance in the monetary sysieui gave ground to fear the slackening of business, and the diminution of employment. Well, thanks to your aid, and to the energy displayed in France and in England þÿ thanks, above alt, to the support of Providence þÿ these dangers, if they have not entirely disappeared, are for the most part dissipated. A great deed of arms has since decided a desperate struggle, unparalleled in history, in favor of the Allies. The opinion of Europe from that moment has been more openly shown. In every direction our alliances have extended, or have become more firm. The third loan has been supplied without difficulty. Tho country has again proved to me its confidence by subscribing a sum

five times larger than I required from it. It has undergone, with admirable resignation, the sufferings inseparable from dearness of provisions þÿ sufferings which, nevertheless, have been mitigated by private charity, by the zeal of the corporations, and by the millions of francs distributed in the departments. An arrival of foreign corn has now produced a considerable fall in the price of food ; the fears arising from the disappearance of gold have faded ; and never has labour been more active, never have the revenues been so large. The chances of war have re-awakened the military spirit of the nation. Never wero there so many voluntary enlistments, nor so great an ardour among the conscripts. To this short statement of our situation I may add a fact of a high political signification. The Queen of Great Britain, wishing to give a proof of her confidence in, and esteem for, our country, and to render our relations still more intimate, came to France. The enthusiastic reception which her Majesty received must have proved to her how deep were the sentiments inspired by her presence, and how much of a character tending to strengthen the alliance of the two peo- O O » pies. The King of Piedmont, who had unhesitatingly embraced our cause with that courageous ardour of which he had previously afforded proof on the field of battle, also came to France to consecrate a union already cemented by the valour of his soldiers. These sovereigns beheld a country, some time so disturbed and fallen from her ranks

in the councils of Europe, now prosperous, peaceable and respected, making war, not with the hurried delirium of passion, but with that calm . which belongs to justice and all the energy of duty. They have seen France, which had sent 200,000 men across the sea, at the same time j convoke at Paris all the Arts of Peace, as if she meant to say to Europe þÿ " The present war is | but an episode for me, and my strength is always in great measure directed towards peaceful occupations. Let us neglect no opportunity of coming to an understanding, and do not force me to throw into the battle-field the whole resources and power of a great nation." This appeal seems to have been heard, and winter, by suspending hostilities, favoured the intervention of diplomacy. Austria resolved upon a decisive step, which brought into the deliberations all the influence of the Sovereign of a vast Empire. Sweden bound herself more closely to England and to France by a treaty, which guaranteed flic integrity of her territory. Finally, from all the Cabinets, advice, or petitions, were sent to St. Petersburg The Emperor of Russia, inheritor of a situation which lie had not brought about, seemed animated by a sincere desire to put an end to the causes which had brought about this sanguinary conflict. He accepted determinedly (avec determination) the propositions transmitted by Austria The honor of arms once satisfied, to defer to the distinctly expressed wish of Europe, was to do himself honour.

At this moment the Plenipotentiaries of the belligerent and Allied Powers are met at Paris to decide on the conditions of peace. The spirit of | moderation and equity, which animates them all, must make us hope for a favorable result. Ne- i vertbeless, let us, with dignity, wait for the end I of the Conference ; and let us bo equally ready, if it prove necessary, to unshcath the sword again, or to offer the hand of friendship to those with whom we have honourably fought. Whatever happen, let us busy ourselves with all matters which tend to augment the power and the wealth of France. Let us draw still closer, if that be possible, the alliance which has been formed by a common participation in glory and in sacrifices, and of which peace will make the mutual advantages appear even more con-

Let us, lastly, at this moment, so solemn for the destinies of the world, put our trust in God, so that He may guide our effort-- in a way the most advantageous to the interests of humanity and of civilisation. Kingston Jamaica, Jan. 11. þÿ A public meeting was held on the 11th instant, at Kingston, for the purpose of taking into consideration the necessity of providing for the repair of large vessels, by the erection of a patent slip, a floating dock, or otherwise. There were present several of the most important members of the mercantile community. Mr. R. J.C. Hitchens was called to the chair, þÿ Captain Cooper said, he had no doubt that if a floating dock were to be imported, the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company would expend to the amount of from 1000/. to 1,500/. per annum on it, for the repair of their steamers. He then went on to speak of the inconvenience of repairing the Company's steamers at New York and Bermuda þÿ the cost for docking at the former place being fully 100/. per day ; and the approach to the latter being both intricate and dangerous. For these reasons, the company, as well as the naval authorities would prefer to have their vessels docked in Jamaica, where they could be done more cheaply, and with greater safety. He was of opinion, that situated as Jamaica is with respect to the isthmus, over which an immense traffic must shortly he carried a floating dock in Kingston Harbour, in which the largest steamers could be repaired, would do far more to render the island prosperous, by holding out an inducement for vessels to come here than even the abolition of the Tonage Dues Several other gentlemen followed, in support of Cap-

tain Cooper's views; and an opinion was expressed that the British government might he induced to grant a sum of money for the carrying out of an underiaking which would be so beneficial to slops of war. þÿ On motion of Mr. Girod, the two following resolutions " Resolved wen: put and unanimously agreed to: þÿ þÿ That in the opinion of this meeting would greatly conduce to the it Commercial prosperity of Kingston, and promote the Maritime interests of the structed, Island, were a dock or slip to he con- i i i!i - of receiving the largest steameis visiting our port. That a committee he appointed for the purpose of preparing a prospectus, and communicating with the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty and the Directors of the Royal Mail Steam-packet Company, with a view to ascertain to what extent they would he respectively willing to contribute to such an object." þÿ Shipping & Mercantile Gazette.

Inter-Colouial. DEMERARA. ( From the Royal Gazette , March I ) . By far the worst aspect of the late riots presents itself when we regard them as indications of the intellectual and moral stale of the mass of the community. How very combustible the moral material must be, when causes apparently so very inadequate can set it in such a blaze. We certainly knew before that the masses of our labouring population were grossly ignorant, and that, as a natural consequence, their consciences were not particularly acute, but we certainly were not prepared for the total want of principle which the late occurrences have brought to light. When a few designing scoundrels, themselves ignorant, can in a day or two convert hundreds of peaceable men, women.

'SlttDU A T H 3. and children into house-breakers, thieves, and rioters, it is clear enough they have found very apt pupils, and that the moral material can he easily fashioned to evil. The rioters had nothing to complain of, not one substantial grievance to make a handle of, nor were they suffering under privation or general calamity of any kind. In thickly populated countries where labour is sometimes cheap and provisions dear, and can dull seasons the working man where in with difficulty procure the bare necessaries of life, and is sometimes even on the border of starvation, there is something to account for riotous proceedings. But there is nothing ot that kind in the present case. Labour is well remunerated, and in great request, Provisions are plentiful, and can he had at prices quite commensurate with the with wages. A man or a woman, rate ot iio other qualifications than bodily health and a pair of hands, can with ease, not only proe sustenance but live comfortably, and with a small portion of prudence and foresight, could save a portion of wages and gradually accumulate comforts around them. There is, therefore, nothing to complain of on that score. The laws, too, are equally administered, and inercitully too. No one can deny that. There is no shadow of partiality on account of rank or colour. All classes enjoy a freedom such as British subjects alone enjoy. Taxation is by no means grievous, and effects only indirectly and in a slight degree the class referred to. In the absence, then,

of any other apparent cause, we are obliged, in accounting for these lawless doings, to fall back upon the two causes which are the root of the whole evil, namely, the gross that fearful immorality our labouring population. ignorance and the prevail is among It one good we have obtained out of all the mischief, that the existence ot these two evils has been, as it were, forced upon the attention of all of us, and we will sin fearfully if we shut our eyes to them. For the existence of these evils to the present time, and for the extent to which they exist, we fear we are all to blame more or less. The sins ot our fathers have no doubt been visited on us in some degree, and our own have been punished too. þÿ Little was done to prepare the slave for freedom, and little has been done to fit him for it since, and these doings are quite the legitimate consequences of the neglect. \N e are quite aware of the difficulties in the way of education, secular and religious, and of the time required to bring it to bear upon the masses of a community such as ours; but we trust it will now he seen that money spent in tills way is economically spent, and that it is ten thousand times better to spend it liberally in enlightening the minds and informing the consciences of men, and thus making them capable of ruling themselves, than to be forced to spend it in compensating the sufferers from lawless outrage, and in salaries to a double allowance of policemen. Never, we believe, in a partially civilized country has

any evil occurred so purely the offspring of ignorance and nothing else. There is one feature in the riotous proceedings in Georgetown which deserves notice. Whence came all those women we saw among the crowd. Out of what holes did they come? and where have they burrowed again? What are their occupations aud their means of support? Have these creatures homes? Are they wives? Are they daguhters? Are they mothers? We need hardly ask their characters. Crea-

tures more shameless, lost to every sense of decency, we have never seen. We have seen riots in several countries, but certainly none in which this very disgusting feature appeared so prominently. It is well known the women were the leaders and the instigators of all the mischief. We have heard of one or two cases in which the men were actu ally shamed into these outrages against their own better reason by the women. Surely the moral atmosphere in which these people live is fearfully pestilential when woman, the natural conservative of peace, is the first to break the peace, and the prominent actor in such scenes as these. If these are the women who share the homes of our labourers, what must those homes be? Willi regard to Georgetown especially, we had not the slightest idea that there were half the number of lewd, abandoned women in it, till the sound of Mr. Orr's trumpet brought them forth. We would respectfully enquire of our City Clergy whether they knew of it, and whether any steps have been taken in time past to investigate the evil and to apply the remedy. If not, it is surely full time to begin. We are aware of the fewness of their numbers, and the wide extent of the duties of each of them ; hot they have lately shewn that in times of trouble and civil disorder they can write and stand side by side against the progress of evil. Would it not be well for them to consider whether they could not act together always without compromising any principle or opinion worth contend-

ing for, and whether by cordially recognising each other's presence and usefulness, and dividing the labour fairly, they could not do that thoroughly and effect ually which can at present be done only very imperfectly ; as, for instance, a general missionary visitation of the lower classes in the City. No one denomination could do it well, hut all denominations working together could do it thoroughly.

PRUSSIA. þÿ A proposition has been laid before the Prussian Chamber making two demands , one, that the question of the Sound Dues should be entered on, seeing that the present treaty is about to expire ; the other, that an end should be to the Russian prohibitory system and its close frontier, with guarantees for the future Accounts from Berlin state that the Czar will throw no impediments in the way of peace, as the want of money and men is becoming more manifest to the Russian Government, and the in tention of the Czar to devote himself to the development of the internal resources of his empire is openly talked of in the most august circles. TURKEY. þÿ -The decree, making concessions to the Christians, and promulgated on the 21st February, states that Europeans will havearight to possess lauded property ; and that, as regards civil lights, there will be a complete equality between Mussulmans and Christians. Any denomination of a nature to express the superiority of one race over another is expressly forbidden The patriarchs are to be named for life. The clergy will receive a fixed stipend, and the Church property will be managed by an assembly composed of persons of that religion. There will be mixed tribunals. Education will be free, but under the surveillance of mixed commissions Other reforms are announced, as, for iustanee, the right granted to provincial and communal councils to take the initiative in grants for public works ; as also the establishment of banks, in

order to regularise the monetary system of the empire. ENGLAND. þÿ The British þÿParliament. House of Commons. þÿ The Preliminaries of Peace. þÿ Mr. Disraeli inquired whether it was true, as reported, that the preliminaries of peace bad been signed at Paris. Lord Palmerston replied that, as the House was aware, certain articles had been proposed bv Austria to Russia, with the previous consent of England and France, as conditions to serve as the foundation of a treaty of peace. These conditions were at first accepted by Russia, with a reservation, and afterwards unconditionally, or pure and simple. These articles were subsequently recorded in a protocol at Vienna, signed by the Plenipotentiaries When the Conferences commenced at Paris, it was agreed at the first meeting that the previous protocol should be inserted in the proceedings of that day, and it had been determined that that protocol and the articles which had been accepted should have the force and value of a preliminary treaty of peace That was the precise state of the matter. No treaty of the ordinary form of a preliminary treaty had been signed

FREEDOM IN TURKEY (From the Illustrated London News, March 8.) A grand ceremony took place at Constantinople on the 21st of last month. At three o'clock on that day there assembled at the Porte the Grand Vizier, all the Ministers, all the members of the Council of State, all the chief functionaries of the Government, the Sheik-ul-Islam or Chief Mahometan Priest, the Patriarchs, Archbishops and Bishops, who are the heads of the different religious communities in Turkey, a large number of the most conspicuous men resident in Constantinople, of different, nations ard professing different creeds ; and at that hour there gathered round the Palace a considerable crowd from every part of the capital. There and then was read by the Chief Secretary in the þÿ of the Grand Vizier, Habat Effendi, whose name is worthy of being remembered, an Imperial Firman, or New Grand Charter for Turkey, placing all the sabjects of the Sultan, of whatever religion, on an equal footing. After the reading tho Sbeik-ul-Islaru pronounced an appropriate prayer, appealing to the one God who reigns over all and everywhere, who is worshipped by Mahometans as by Christians, to bless and consecrate the freedom and equal rights which the Sultan granted to all his people. A solemn earnestness, a good omen of success, as indicating that all parties felt their responsibility, and that the ceremony was more than show, marked the whole proceeding. Even the crowd outside was awed, and received with veneration the firman signed
by tho Sultan. Everybody, we are told by eye-witnesses, seemed penetrated with the solemnity of the moment, and to be aware that ha

was assistiug at the birth of freedom for many nations. " The consecration which the rights of the empire have received from the benevolent and friendly assistance of the Great Powers, the Sultan's noble allies" one is of the reasons assigned for now extending religious and political freedom j there is no talk of his coming, as was amongst all his subjects, of whatever religion or race. All rights and privileges previously grant- ; tismal ceremony, and we are assured ed to non-Mussulman communities are confirmed and maintained Fixed incomes are to be substituted for ecclesiastical dues, and all the property of Christian and other communities will be placed under their own laymen and clergy. New churches and places worship may of be erected, when police considerations the erection ; and all is to be done in are not opposed " to a spirit of charity and tolerance," while the freest exercise of every religion is guaranteed to all. From the official vocabulary all epithets, and from official dealings all distinctions, are to be excluded, which remind classes of old oppressions) and are of themselves rankling insults, and are to be abolished for ever. All offices are to be opened to the Sultan's subjects, according to their capacities ; and, to fit the humblest for the highest places, schools for art and science are encouraged Justice is to be publicly administered þÿ no longer bought and sold ; and men of different creeds will be partly under the jurisdiction and protection of judges of their own faith. A code of laws and rules for the adminis-

tration of justice in mixed courts, are promised, and are to be published not kept locked up in þÿ unintelligible jargons, as is the case in one civilised country that we know þÿ in all the languages used in the empire. Prisons are to be substituted for filthy dungeons, and torture is to be abolished, as the slave, trade has already been prohibited. All are to be equally liable to defend the country, which implies that all may bear arms ; and, while all are made equally subject to taxation, all are to be protected from official robbery. The taxes will not hereafter be collected at the point of the sabre ; and, in impos- ; ing them, care is to be taken not to make them impediments to the development of trade. Military service is to be commuted for money. Roads and canals and banks are all promised ; and, under the beneficial influence of private enterprise, some of these are already begun. These stipulations, promises, and guarantees are as yet, indeed, little more than words, and men do not now need to learn that the bestdrawn charters do not confer freedom. This is rather to be won than granted. Nevertheless, as laying principles and rules worthy to be followed, as acknowledging limits which ought to be enforced on arbitrary power, and so creating a safe guide to a better future, honoured þÿ at least nominally þÿ by Pachas and Rajahs, the granting of this Charter is to be set down in our histories as the commencement of a new era in the moral life of all Mussulman nations. Nor

can it be otherwise than beneficial in Western Europe that the high principles of its own political morality, which are far more generally taught by its sages than acted on by its rulers, are echoed in the East and come back to affright despotic rulers and encourage people in struggling for freedom. When there is moral progress in Turkey there can be no lagging behind in Christendom. It seems now tolerably certain, from the general craving for moral improvement, from the fact that of late prodigious advances have been made in all the mechanic arts and sciences, and from the fact that one kind of improvement is ever the parent of another þÿ a common growth being necessary to preserve the general harmony þÿ that the coming age is to be one of general moral progress, and of this progress the charter of religious and political freedom now drawn up for Turkey is one of the many signs. We must add, to do proper honour to an individual, that the Grand Vizier, Mehcmet Emir Aali Pacha is charged with the execution of the ordinance, and is the Minister to whom the credit is due of having counselled and prepared it.

disgraceful secrets. CHINA. þÿ According to the advices by the last overland mail, the Chinese rebellion appears to be making head against the Government. In Kwangsi, the rebels have been succeisful, and have entirely possessed themselves of three prefectures in the province of Kiangsi, which threatens to interrupt the transit from the tea and silk producing country. In the north, also, the province of Honan is said to be in a state of insurrection, but no particulars of the movement have yet been received. There is also a report that a plague has broken out at Chin-kiang-foo, and carried off upwards of 100,000 persons. It is called the black-tongue plague, from its peculiar symptoms At Canton, all remains quiet, but the progress of the rebels is a source of uneasiness.

NEW WARLIKE INVENTIONS. A letter form St. Petersburg, of the says : þÿ In its late sittings the Naval Education Commission has been much occupied by the examination and consideration of several new discoveries and inventions connected with war. Amongst others, a Mr. Pahl produced a liquid substance capable of burning on the surface of the water, and with which he proposes to set the enemy's ships on fire, and another which ignites of itself by being set free in the open air if the temperature be above 15deg. (66 deg. of Fahrenheit). On this latter liquid the inventor laid great stress, as being applicable in successfully checking attacks of cavalry. The former was subjected to a long investigation, but ultimately declined, as it was not found to burn with sufficient power to set hostile ships on fire, and was moreover liable to be easily extinguished by the winds and action of the waves. The latter was also considered not practical, and declined. Then there were several projects for building ships to sail under water, a new invention for destroying enemy's ships submitted by a Dutchman of the name of Tetterode, and finally a commission on the first of January, 1856, ) plan for fixing submarine palisades by a Mr. Dade. Some of these were rejected as impracticable, and others ordered to be further considered.

From the London Weekly Dispatch. At length the subject of the Baltic operations has been brought before the House by Sir Charles Napier. The old Admiral is not exactly the person to set his own cause in the most artistical light, or to take up the most unassailable logical position. But he has done his work. His adversaries are driven to the most pitiful personal retort, and to the abandonment of all such grounds of defence as might serve them for anything like a fair acquittal. Indeed, it is not necessary to read Sir Charles Napier's speech at all to come to the certain conclusion that the Admiralty, and Sir James Graham in particular, have been grosdy deficient in their plainest duties. We will take the simple instance of the gun-boats. If you had reported to us, says Sir James Graham to Sir Charles Napier, in the month of May, 1S54, the plan by which Swcaborg could have been destroyed, you could have been furnished with the means in the course of that very season. Sir Charles replies that he was not within a hundred miles of Sweaborg in t lie month of May, and, therefore, could nut furnish the report he afterwards made. But the plan he did recommend as effectual was the employment of a great many gun-boats þÿ 200 was the number afterwards used in the correspondence. Now, if Sir James Graham could have got 200 gun-boats ready in the summer of 1854, how is it that he could not get that number forward for tho opening of the Baltic in 1855 ? How is it that we find him driven to the wretched plea that there were then sent forward 26 gun-

boats, 22 mortar-vessels, and 5 floating batteries þÿ 53 in all, which, had the French reinforced them with a like number, would have given but 106 ? We all know that the French directed their force of small vesse's to the B'ack Sea, so that, in fact, the allies had about a third of the number of vessels required for this sort of squadron in the Baltic after nearly a year's notice, and, by that very weakness, the complete demolition of Sweaborg was prevented ; and we were obliged to put up with a gallant demonstration instead of a perfect and telling success. The sham of preparations at home gave us the sham victory abroad, and a sham one only. This is the main subject ; the means of conquest were not provided whon there were ample warning and ample time ; and Sir Charles Napier is perfectly borne out in his assertion, by the very plea of the person ho accuses, that had the Emperor Nicholas beon at tho head of tho British Admiralty, he would scarcely have done better for

3 ® 'It VI XL ATIS, Russia than our First Lord Let Sir James Graham, Mr. Osborne, Admiral Berkeley, and all the parties implicated, get over the effect of their own statement, if they can. The very armament we are now boasting of convicts them. The numbers now getting ready lor sea are those discussed and accepted as necessary in 1854 The naval power of England is disgraced in its results by this deliberate procustiuation and neglect, this virtual " treason." If we are to go into the person d matter, the defence appears as pitiful in spirit as feeble iu effect. Sir Charles Napier is accused by Sir James Graham of soliciting the command of the Baltic fleet. No doubt he desired it, aud with a most justifiable ambition. But surely Sir James will not dare to say that he gave the command upon any other consideration than that of the good of the service and of the country. He now brings forward Sir C. Napier's formerly printed opinions, that an Admiral after 60 years of age loses his nerve. But Sir James is concluded from this wretched argument by his own act arid deed. It is no fault of Sir Charles Napier's to grow old. It is a great fault in a Minister to employ Sir Charles if he thinks him too old. Sir Charles Napier, on being appointed to a fleet inferior far in numbers to the Russian one, short of hands, and manned, as far as it was manned, in many instances with those who had never been at sea, honourably places his difficulties on record before he sets sail. Sir James turns upon him, and says, in fact þÿ " Oh ! if you don't like ycur fleet,

you had better resigu." No, rejoins the Admiral þÿ and now we quote verbatim þÿ " I should consider myself a coward and unworthy of holding her Majesty's commission, were I to decline any service, be it ever so desperate ." And this is the written language which Sir James quotes to show that a proper aud sufficient fleet was provided, and that the responsibility so far was taken by Sir Charles Napier! As to Almifal Berkeley, he is not content with heaping all sorts of contumely on the discarded Admiral who is supposed to have no friends, for his conduct in the Baltic ; he actually goes back to the bombardment of Acre, and tries to prove that, so far from Sir C Napier's bearing there being strictly meritorious, it was positively dctremental to the attack. Sir Charles, of course, answered this at full. But take the case us Admiral Berkeley states it. Admiral Berkeley was at Acre. Admiral Berkeley was a Lord of the Admiralty when Sir C. Napier was appointed to the Baltic command Admiral Berkeley knew then what lie knows now, and if ho now speaks the truth, he must have considered Sir Charles Napier an utter importer. Yet so far from interposing to prevent the appointment of this imposter to tho roost important naval command ever conferred in England, Admiral Berkeley dined at the Reform Club dinner to fete the newly selected commander, and, in the House of Commons, declared that it was his own highest ambition to command the Baltic fleet, but that he felt it a duty to his country to yield his claims to the

man whom all concurred in naming as fittest for the honour and the duty. When the defenders set this seal to their own case, the nation need not look to the accusations of their opponent. There they stand, utterly, hopelessly self-convicted. Sir Charles Napier may have committed some errors ; his memory may not serve him on a few secondary points ; his age may not have left him vigorous and unshaken as he was 20 years ago. But really the most serious imputation upon him as a leader is his own admission, that while he was in the Baltic he had the gout, and was thereby kept back in one instance from a personal reconnaissance The House of Com-

mons was in no humour to grant him his committee. That, perhaps, is of no great cousequence just now, when we arc but too much occupied with the investigation of other delinquencies. But it is not lie who needs further investigation for the clearing of his character. In spite of all the practised rhetoric brought against him, he has won his cause on the substantial merits, and exposed the maladministration of the Admiralty in a fashion that will certainly not tempt its successors hastily to repeat its unpardonable faults, or the iusolcnt, disingenous aud thoroughly-unsuccessful style of defending them. i :: lM i;, The most interesting feature of intelligence is the birth of an Imperial Prince, which took place tit the Palais Itoyale, at Paris, yesterday morning at halt-past G. The Czar knows that he is not a Nicholas ; and it is an off-set against the advantages of a despotism, that so much depends on the despot, just as with free countries, it is an offset against their had administrations, that the public zeal can do good service. Not only is he not a Nicholas, hut he lias lost the flower of his father's troops, and of his Southern possessions. I Itwill make all the concessions he dare, all that his subjects will let him. He will do so precisely in proportion as he finds the English people ready to fight. The moment there is a " hitch" þÿ and we shall he sure to hear something authentic Men, for our Ministry will whistle to its " public," as a man in

danger does to his dog þÿ people must he reaily to speak out. It it he " Nicolaieff," we must he as steady as granite. No peace till the Bug is harmless ! Our navy has not yet had its turn, and it longs for it. Every sailor feels that the red-jacket has beaten the blue-jacket ; and that John Bull is grumbling at his favourite profession. We have troops well capable of maintaining their present position þÿ all things considered, no mean one. And it is the blue-jackets' turn next. So that we need he in no eagerness to avoid a fresh struggle ; and not let the re-action which naturally occurs during the lull of an armistice overcome our energy too far. This readiness is not incompatible with the most pol ite willingness to accept an honourable peace, on such terms as we have a right to believe Russia intends to offer, by offering negotiations at all. We make these remarks, because we observe that the universal talk of peace has made thousands fancy peace certain; while fancy maks them languid about all war chances, which languor helps the diplomatists of Russia. In the interval, we are at our old business þÿ a general overhaul of the British nest for the instruction of Europe. It is all very well for the hacks ci bunglers to tell us, a la "Saturday S'.tivievv," that we had best hold our : <ngues, for fear of disgracing ourselves abroad. The fact is, that it is an founding proof of our vitality, and an encouraging symptom, that our system bears this publicity so well. Besides

which, we are all very well aware, that io hold our tongues is to ensure our destruction, and that to expose our blunders is the only chance we have of mending them and the lesser of the two Fvtls. We were very glad of Mr. Roct.JCk's debate of the 29lh ult. We admit that the Opposition is perfectly right ut present in not joining Mr. Roebuck. But the country ought to have the gcperal facts well brought before

S 0 & C) 1 & ATS 3 them. Let us have no scandalous hypocrisy. We have disgraced ourselves, and honoured the people who have helped us, and the whole affair is very curious as a study. Let us turn to the very interesting motion" in question, " though it was withdrawn. The motion is gone ; hut the system it exposed, is here: and the whole debate was instructive. It was rich in facts which nobody can deny, and which nobody seems likely to remedy. Sir de Lacy Evans is a man whose experience has been great, and whose veracity is unquestionable. What does he tell us? 1st, That when Colonel Gordon said the ' general officers refused to receive the knapsacks," he said what could not he proved. 2nd, That the losses from sickness were in some cases 50 or 60 per cent., so that we need not wonder facts are kept hack. 3rd, That one regiment (apparently the 46th) was landed in heavy rains, with nobody to receive it, and nearly disappeared. 4th, That lime-juice was kept " returns" in such medical matters are hack, while scurvy was raging, and that still suppressed. 5th, That officers were put in charge of high and important departments, who had not been in the field for 20, or even sometimes 40, years. 6th, That Colonel Gordon, the deputy-Quarterniasler-General, absolutely brought him (Evans) an order to capture a convoy, when no convoy was in the place indicated, and to go there, would have caused useless slaughter. 7th, That the Turkish Contingent was absurdly ordered about from place to place. 8lli, That Dragoons were sent

to Kertch, a place unfit for cavalry, and afterwards, by a series of blunders, kept 29 days on hoard ship. Now, why detail these facts? Because people are too careless to read them when spread over three columns of the "Times"; and because Lord Palmerston could absolutely make no answer to this important speech, except that it was "of a personal character"; as if that was not its inevitable character, and its value into the bargain, llow on earth criticise men's doings without criticising men ? Or, are the horses and the gun-carriages to blame, and not " persons" at all ? Lord C. Hamilton turned on the General, with the accusation that he had advised Raglan to retreat after Inkerman. The General showed that the accusation was overdone; and we do not at all wonder that Sir de Lacy should have advised what he did. He may think now, that his advice was as weil not followed, hut that is no reason he should repeat that advice. There is a case exactly in point, told by Plutarch of Phocion, though we do not wonder it never occurred to Lord C. Hamilton! His "vindication" of Colonel Gordon resolved itself into a transfer of the blunder to the shoulders of Raglan, who, being dead, is of course a safe man to blame- Considering that Government had the Report which occasioned this discussion, seven months on hand, it is wonderful they have got up the case no better. Here we had Palmerston justifying the Cardigan appointment, on the ground of an anonymous authority's having called

him "a good cavalry officer" ; as if we did not know that his cavalry starved under his command. In fact, the Premier justifies his appointments in the teeth ol the Report of the Commission ; and says we ought not to anticipate the coming "board of general officers,"

when the very point in debate is, whether that hoard is a proper tribunal. This is begging the question with a vengeance ! We doubt whether a handful of prejudiced old men is a proper tribunal ; and we are told that we must wait tor the judgment of the old men. This is an insult to our common sense, as the blunders above-mentioned were to our national honour. It is well known that the hoard is to consist of orthodox, old military pedants (and no pedant is worse than a military one), who will view the matter entirely from the point of view of the men inculpated. They are to turn out the public whenever they please ; that is, whenever it is most the interest of the public to he present. Nor is it clear what their powers are, and what they are going to decide. In fact, the officers to whose " explanations" they are to listen, ought to have been brought to a court-martial long since, when iheir shameful want of military conduct was first shown. Byng was shot tor conduct which in our time would have ensured Ins being made Lord High Admiral. This is not a flourish ot rhetoric, hut a plain and proveable fact. We are not at all apprehensive that these discussions will imperil the peace. It is, indeed, right, in point of forms, for great parties not to embarrass the ministry while negotiations are in progress ; hut, that the country, in the widest sense, should show its disgust at past block headisnt, and its zeal for future energy, is a phenomenon rather favourable to peace than otherwise. When

potentates see that we hate and repudiate the mediocrities who have disgraced lis, and mean to have better men for the future, they will augur well of our persistency, and be likely to concede our rights. If we cannot get better men, let us know the worst at once, and face it. But we do not believe that England is "used up" yet, though Mr. F. Peel is in office; and though fools and cowards employ the present interval of sus pense in truckling to powers which can only he awed by cheerful resolution.

They also recommended that the 10th paragraph should read thus : " The newspapers of the Danish Westindia Islands may be ordered at the post offices on the payment of 10 pr. Ct., in addition to the costprice. Otherwise transmission of newspapers between the Islands and between the Islai. Is and the Mother Country are exempted from payment ment." of all post charges to the Danish post depart- This advice has been passed unnoticed by the members of the Danish Diet ; and here we see the great advantage of having a consultative assembly for the purpose of giving advice in regard to local matters on which the members are supposed to have some knowledge ; which advice is paid little regard to by those who possess no knowledge whatever of such matters We can scarcely see the use of this lawhaving been laid before the Colonial Council, when its most objectionable points were to be enforced regardless of the amendments proposed by that assembly. However, we must believe when we are told, that " we are unripe for self-government."

The following oration was delivered somewhere in Wisconsin, by one of the profession, who would seem to have quite þÿ " May it please your an aversion to capital punishment : lordship and gentlemen of the jury, þÿ the cause is as clear as ice, and sharp to the point as ' No' from your sweetheart. Gentlemen, murder is murder whether committed by twelve jurymen, or by an humble individual like my client. Gentlemen, I do not deny the fact of my client having killed a man, hut is that any reason why you should do so ; No such thing, gentlemen ; you may bring the prisoner in' guilty;' the hangman may do his duty, hut will that exonerate you ? goblins of despair Gentlemen, beware of committing murder! Beware, I say, of meddling with the eternal prerogative! Beware, I say. THE COLONIAL COUNCIL. We made no mention of the election for Membets to the Colonial Council prior to its taking place, as we had heard that on this occasion a number of voters would record their votes in order to prove to the Governments, whether European or Colonial, that the non-voting heretofore did not arise from indifference to the benefits which the Institution was amply calculated to bestow on the inhabitants of these Colonies, buf from the conviction that in selecting men whose prominent positions in the Island render them competent to comprehend our interests and wants ; it would be only a fruitless proceeding, in as much as the personal interests of those men hold them to the place, and in moving away to another Island for a public cause, they are too surely sacrificing their own þÿ Self-preservation is the first law of þÿnature, and it is too much to expect otherwise iu our circle. It is said that a meeting of the Colonial Council will take place this month (April), and that questions highly important to St. Thomas will there be discussed Now what is our position ? The mere choice of the month shows that St. Croix does not understand us We are at the end of a severe commercial crisis ; a neighbouring Island, with which we have large transactions, has passed through an epidemic term, during which time our relation? almost ceased ; it is only a commercial city that can know how commerce has been deranged by such a circumstance, and what must be the pulse of men on whose minds rest the weight of

sueh a suspension to trade. It is not only that remittances for goods do not come, but the Ex change market gets adrift and exigencies have to Let some influential Planter or other benevo- j be provided for on all sides. Is it likely that men so situated, who anxiously look just now for every daily Mail to be informed of their affairs, in many cases, no doubt, unsatisfactory, could be persuaded to go away to participate in publie matters ? No doubt had St. Thomas possessed the right to convene a meeting she would have done so two months ago, when the Island was at leisure, and the discussions in the Council would have formed an agreeable gossip for the town, and the members therein enabled to ascertain the opinions of their constituents on matters in debate. Whoever may desire the contrary, we in St. Thomas know practically that a United Council cannot work, unless to our disadvantage Thorefore, let us hope that the same grace which inspired the Sovereign to concede to the Colonies a Consultative Rody, will be the means of bringing to an issue the following from the first section of the law : þÿ þÿ The King may decree its division the one for St. Croix, and (into tho the transaction of all business or ol some particu- other for St. Thomas and St þÿJohn þÿ s for lar branches, and make the provisions, required by this alteration in the present law -St Thomas Times, April 12

We publish in another place the letter of our correspondent þÿ þÿZ, recommending the establishment in this Island of an Asylum or Hospital for Lepers. We are advocates for such an Institution, but would prefer seeing the undertaing started by Government than by private enterprise. If, however, the inhabitants are willing, by subscription, to begin this work, let it be carried through by them ; but not after being once commenced to be taken out of their hands and completed by the Authorities ! We cannot agree with our corresendorse pondent on this one point his opinions. BRITISH PARLIAMENT. HOl'SE OF COMMONS. ARMY þÿCOMMISSIONS. Sir DE- LACY K VANS moved for a select committee to consider, and examine evidence, and report to the House, on the expediency of abolishing the system of sale and purchase of commissions in the Army, and on the means that might he adopted for the accomplishment of that object. He said he trusted the House would pardon him for bringing forward this subject as there were so many in that House more capable than himself of doing so. The gallant General then referred to the arguments used by the supporters of the system of purchase in the army, and to the institution of the system in the reign of Charles II. lie alluded to the French army, where purchase was unknown, and which had not had the effect of producing an inferior class of officers, and also to the Royal Artillery of this country, in which the officers were promoted by merit It had been said by the opponents of the Hill, that it would cost between £8,000,000 and £9,000.00(1 to purchase the commissions of those who had bought their commissions; hut, even admitting this sum would be required, would it not be acting more honourably to those engaged in the service to buy up the commissions than to allow those who were poor to he displaced by others who were in affluent circumstances? He believed the sum stated for this purpose had been exaggerated ; and, at all events, it would not have to be paid down immediately, hut might he extended over several years. He considered that the

country should not he prevented, by pecuniary considerations, from doing an act of justice to those employed in their service. It was a fact, that at present, the actual sum paid for a commission was not its nominal price, which in several cases it greatly exceeded, leaving promotion in the service at the disposal of those who were the most wealthy, and not those who were the most meritorious. In order to secure efficiency for the service, the Army should be thrown open to those who entered it, with the view of adopting it as a profession. Having described the evils that might result to the country from a continuance of the present system in the event of another war, the gallant mem-

3 C ilt'DIZ HT 3, her proceeded. Another reason for altering the present system was the fact that an officer who had no money could seldom obtain promotion, while he who had hut a little money and less influence was not better off. Many officers, in purchasing their commissions, and afterwards their promotion, expended all the money they could procure, either by borrowing from their friends and relatives, or raising it on interest. When they did this, their wives and families, or, if they were unmarried, their mothers and sisturs, were reduced to great privation. He could hardly understate the sufferings of officers who had no money or other means of getting on in the service. In time of war, certainly, many rose rapidly, hut in time of peace it was quite otherwise. It was a melancholy state of things to see an officer, after 15 or 20 þÿyears service, commanded by a young Colonel or Lieutenant Colonel who might have seen only four þÿyears service. (Hear.) There was no doubt whatever that the system would die out of itself, if no commissions were given by purchase. It might he very slow, and, in reducing it to practice, it might lie necessary to make some little addition in the pay, or some retiring allowance ; but no matter what inconvenience might follow, it was monstrous to continue t he present system He appealed to the right lion, member for Buckinghamshire (Mr. Disraeli) and the noble lord at the head of the Government, to consider this important question, and to endeavour to bring it to a speedy and

satisfactory conclusion. The present system was a disgrace to the British Army. With a view to effect a change, he would move for the appointment of a committee to inquire into the subject ; but, it that were not conceded, lie would he satisfied with a commission composed of civil and military men, who would investigate and report upon the subject. The lion, and gallant gentleman, who i classes was scarcely audible, concluded hv reading his motion. Lord PALMERSTON was opposed to the system of purchase, supposing that an army was now about to be constituted for the first time, hut by process of time it had become so intertwined with the military profession that it would he difficult to withdraw it, for in some instances it had been attended with most beneficial results. Without it the Army would be clogged by those who, from age or infirmities, were unable to perform their duties, for, by the system of purchase, a way was opened for younger and more efficient men to obtain promotion by their retirement. If it was abolished, compensation must he made to those who had purchased their commissions, which would lie attended with considerable expense ; but still he thought that the country would not grudge the amount required, as it would he spread over a number of years, if such a cause was deemed to he essential for the well-being of the army. He thought the House seemed to lie agreed that this matter ought to he inquired into, to see if some change could not lie effected; hut he agreed with his right

lion, friend (Mr. Sidney Herbert) that a committee of this House was not the proper tribunal to inquire into it. He said that a commission was the proper body to whom it should he referred, and 1 tory, etc., on with if his lion, and gallant friend would he content with that course on the part of the Government, he was prepared to accede to it. He was willing, on the part of her þÿMajesty s G overnment, to nominate a mixed commission, to whom
should be referred, not only this ques tion, hut that they should inquire into the practice pursued in other countries on this subject.

Fom the London Illustrated Times. THE EXHAUSTION OF RUSSIA. In a daily contemporary appeared the other day a long account by an American, giving þÿ an interior view of þÿRussia. A residence of two years in Russia, extending over a period including the demise of the late Czar, and introductions to all circles, afforded him an opportunity of watching narrowly her resources. As the result of his observations, he gives the following respecting the present exhaustion of Russia, and the importance of striking another blow before she has time to recruit her energies : þÿ þÿ Nicholas is dead. He was the soul of the empire. When his great soul left Russia the great bell cracked. þÿ Russia exhausted the fervour of heroism and the flower of her chivalry at Sebastopol. She cannot during her lifetime, reconstruct the fallen defences of her skill, and she has ceased to be formidable to the enlightened Governments of Europe for the next generation. She has achieved more during the last year or two than she can acheive again for twenty years. Now is the time for the Western Fowers to assert their authority. As time goes on, civilisation may enervate her powers ; vitality will flow into the heart of Russia, and your children may wake up the slaves of the Cossacks. þÿ On the whole, Russia must halt. She has gone on so long in an undisputed career of conquest that the Western nations had good grounds for jealousy, and perhaps alarm. She felt her strength þÿ she did not know her weakness. Her people are suffering, and suffering deeply. All

of subjects are discontented. She cannot continue the war, for her þÿ foes will become those of her own þÿhousehold. She is driven to make peace. Her solid walls of untrained serfs can offer no effectual barriers to the enlightened men who go from the civilised homes of Western þÿEurope.

The schooner þÿ þÿVigilant arrived here mi Sunday last from St. Thomas ; she, however, brought no packet letters or newspapers, þÿ owing to the non-arrival there of the outward steamer when she left, þÿ therefore we are unable to place before our readers to-day any fresh matter in the shape of European (either home or foreign) politics. The þÿ Vigilant left here again yesterday, for St. Thomas, and may be expected back to-night, provided she meets the packet on her arrival there. There exists such a diversity of opinions in our small community, in regard to the question of peace, that we dare not offer one. It is rumoured here, with what truth we cannot vouch, that private letters received a few days ago from the United States of America state that the War had recommenced, and that hostilities were opened between the Allied Powers and Russia ! Let us hope to the contrary, and i rust that the coming mail may be the harbinger of intelligence that will insure the peace of Europe for centuries to come.

Before the issue of our next paper the Members of the Colonial Council will have assembled in the Government House, for the discussion of public affairs þÿ Friday next being the day appointed for the opening of the session.

From the London Weekly Dispatch. The papers just published relative to Kars are voluminous and interesting. It will require and repay much study to trace the entire history of the failure ; but some facts are patent enough at a glance. In the first place the demonstration is complete how impossible it is to carry on effectual war with divided authority. In this ease we have General Williams on the spot, beholding, with bis own eyes, all the necessities of the struggle. At first lie is to communicate with Lord Stratford de Redcliffe only through Lord Raglan, and Lord Stratford is to move the Turkish Government, and our Foreign Minister, Lord Flarendon, who i« to move the War-office and get the permission, in certain cases, of the Em-

3 ii 'Tl 3, peror of the French. General Williams himself appears among the Turkish Pachas only as an adviser, not being furnished by Lord Stratford even with such documents as may show that he is accredited by our Government, and will b# supported by our Embassy in Constantinople, General Williams finds peculation at its height, provision made hopeless by plunder, cowardice in full command. He remonstrates, threatens, but he is laughed at. The Turks see that Lord Stratford refuses to help him. A different plan is evidently entertained in each different place. Notwithstanding all discouragements, General Williams sees the possibility of holding Kars if he were but moderately supported He has proved the truth of his opinion. Lord Clarendon meanwhile was contemplating a retreat to Erzeroum, and a defeat of the þÿenemy army s all the more complete from being the further within the Turkish territory ; the Emperor of the French would not consent to the removal of the Turkish troops from Balaklava, unless they were replaced by others, or the commanders before Sebastopol would say they were not wanted. General Mansfield, the military adviser of our Embassy at Constantinople, anticipated defeat or the giving of ground in Asia, aud only hoped that the entire campaign would give the balance in our favour by success at Sebastopol ; yet he, still not williug to refuse General Williams a chance, kept urging as did the þÿSultan sMinisters, that if Kars could be saved, it must be by employing a part of the loan in furnishing, pay-

ing and equipping the troops, which sum for a long time was not forthcoming from the British Government. Such was the condition of the policy that directs great empires. In the midst of corruption, insolenoe and distress, General Williams held firm. He addressed 62 public dispatches to Lord Stratford de Uedcliffe, and he received no reply. He wrote at last to Lord Clarendon, giving Lord Stratford notice of his so doing, and then a reprimand was sent to the Ambassador. So firm had the General been in his difficulties, that he had concealed Lord þÿStratsford silence s even from his aide-de-camps, as continually awaiting some notice of his communications. When reproved from home, the Ambassador tried to show that he had exerted himself. He might have delayed answering too long, he confessed, as many will think with regard to 62 packets written from a besieged town ; but he had persuaded the Porte to make General Williams a Turkish General of Division, so as to confer authority upon him with the Pachas ; and the commander at Kars then obeyed the General, though Selim Pacha, the notorious paltroon that should have marched from Erzeroum, refused to stir. The latter facts are all within the memory of newspaper readers. Now, giviug its full weight to the thorough misorganization of all possible plans by the cross influence of all manner of authorities, and full of his own ideas aud ordering what would mar every other project, or, at the very least, not rendering the slightest help where help was of vital con-

sequence, a main issue remains between General Williams and Lord Stratford de Rodcliffo. His lordship, who the other day was described as lecturing the Sultan himself in most unseemly fashion, appears, when the cowardly, corrupt, traitorous Pachas are in question, suddenly struck with an amazing respect for the Turkish character. Of Lord Clarendon he þÿ ventures to ask whether the tone which General Williams has assumed towards them þÿ the abruptness of his charges þÿ the violence of his threats þÿ the dictatorial spirit which, according to his own account, has generally characterised his proceedings þÿ can be said to correspond with that intention, or to favour those dispositions to reform, which it is our object to produce no less at Kars than throughout the Turkish empire þÿ One of the scoundrels of whose honor and feelings the Ambassador was so tender had been drawing rations for 35,000 men, when there were only 14,000 He was accused of rotting away his army to profit thus by the dead Indeed the whole conduct of the Turkish commanders, until General Williams made himself obeyed, has long been in print before the British public, and its striking points shall soon be reproduced in these columns General Williams was toiling unsupported where any one else would have despaired, aud Lord Stratford, even if we accept his own defence to Lord Clarendon, was treating his 62 or rather 124 unanswered letters, as full of þÿ much superfluous and exaggerated þÿmatter, the Ambassador
not oven condescending to express a desire that he might he furnished with shorter reports and promising to attend to them A more sickening

spectacle of arrogant wilfulness, a sadder catas trophe brought about by a no-system of blunder, a more hapless neglect of all that is noble in sham deference to the preposterously base, never disgraced the annals of the world. There is no relief in the picture but in the heroism of the man who lies, we fear, at the gasp of death brought upon him by these injuries ; there can be uo satisfaction but in making it signally impossible that the folly and wickedness should ever be repeated.

It nm'ds not fortune to be groat While there's a coin surpassing gold No matter whieh way Fortune leans. Wealth makes not happiness secure . Stern Fate the greatest still enthralls, And Misery hath Its high compeers ; For Sorrow enters palace halls, And Queens are not exempt from tears. The princely robe and beggar's coat, The scythe and sword, the plume and plough. Are in the grave of equal note þÿ Men live but iu the eternal " Now I"

But grasp thou Truth, though bleak appears The rugged path her steps have trod ; She'll he thy friend in other spheres þÿ Companion in the world of God.

Many are the complaints that we daily hear uttered in reference to the new postal law ; but none of the grievances we think so serious to our commercial men, though few they be, than the delay in the deliverance of letters, þÿ&c., owing, no doubt, to the insufficiency of assistants in the Post Office. The schooner " Scholten" arrived here at 5 o'clock 011 Wednesday afternoon, and the letters brought by her were delivered as lute as 8 o'clock the following morning. One merchant, we learn, had to call personally 011 the Postmaster, and beg as a tavor to have delivered to him a letter which was of great importance to him. This is certainly grievous. The new postal law is as complex in every particular it out are as limited as they could carrying as any : yet the arrangements for possibly be. Is the object of the law solely lor the gaining of a large revenue, or is the Post Office lor the public benefit ? The latter can scared)' be the case when the new post office arrangements are contemplated. Beyond a few labelled boxes and some stamps we see no other arrangements made that could insure regularity and expedition !

We learn that Messrs. Rothschild, Schiin and Hingelberg, who came passengers in the schooner " Vigilant," form a deputation from the inhabitants of St Thomas, to confer with the Governor on the grievances arising out of the new postal system, with a view, if possible, to their removal. His Excellency received the deputation yesterday at Government House ; and we have been promised a sketch of the result of the interviews with His Excellency þÿ when we hope to place the same before the public. We commend our sister-island 011 this most praise-worthy move, and look forward to the example being followed here.

On a perusal of the Ordinance I find that article B, paragraph 15, page 215 fays þÿ "Foreign letters shall, on their arrival, immediately be delivered to the Post Office." Well, our foreign correspondence must thus be conveyed to the Post Office, which is carried there free of cost toil, and it then undertakes to deliver within a radius of not much more than a quarter of an English mile our despatches, at a cost of 4c., 8c., 16c.
