There was no regular sitting of the Conferences on Saturday, but M Walewski assembled bis colleagues that day in order to read to them the protocols which will serve as the bases to the treaty of definitive peaco. A commission composed of the following members was named to draw up the treaty : Lord Cowley, for England ;

M de Bourqueney, for France ; Baron de Bruuow, for hussia ; M. de Hulmer, for Austria ; mid Aali Piielia, for Tut key Sardinia and Prussia are unrepresented The Iiidrptndunce Beige states that, when peace shall have been signed, it is intended that the Conference shall bv- dissolved, but that a committee shall be left sitting to carry out the details, which there is not now time to arrange The que tiotts of the Principalities and of the Turkish Christians will probably receive the uttentiou of this budy. Front all that can be learned in respectable quarters there appears little doubt that peace is all but decided. There may he certain points »t il to settle, certain toi m.tliues to fulfil, but they are not of a character to affect the certainty of the result, or hardly to retard it The Russians are described as now presenting no serious difficulty, whether as regards the "neutralisation" of the Black Sea, or the transformation of Nicolaieff into a purely commercial port, the neutrality of the Aland l.-les, the rectification of the Moldavian frontier based on the report of a commission, i$C. There will be several matters to regulate after the signing of the treaty, but an easy solution is anticipated. Such, at all events, is the general feeling Whether the peace will be durable or not is another question. It may he doubted if all the plenipotentiaries are as well satisfied with the results as people pretend to be. If one could guess what passes in the mind of M de Cavour, for instance, his delight is far from ex-

cessive. If Couut Buol were to speak his thoughts, he is probably neither over-pleased nor over-flatte ed at the result. The object which Russia at this moment scorns and hates the most on earth is Austria. When Couut Esterbuzy last saw the Czar at St. Petersburg, the latter said, " Is it Austria that has forced me to accept such hard conditions ? Be assured, and tell your master what I say, 1 shall never forget the obligations 1 owe him." This is a pretty state of feeling for peacemakers ! In the meantime, so confident are people in Paris of peace being virtually concluded, that at the War Office measures are discussed for the best and most convenient way of bringing hack the troops from the Crimea M. de Manteuffel, the Prussian Plenipotentiary, attended the conferences with M. de Hatzfeldt. The sitting of the Conference announced for Wednesday, last week, was countermanded. The meeting broke up at half-past throe ; and the plenipotentiaries then walked up end down in the garden, smoking cigars. Aali Pacha, like a true Turk, smoked a pipe, but still a French pipe, very short. The Siecle conveys intelligence from St. Petersburg which shadows forth, according to this authority, some of tho leading articles of the expected treaty. 1. Russia consents to the neutralisation of the Black Sea. 2. Sehnstopul is not again to become a war depot, and the reconstruction of the fortresses is prohibited 3. Nicolaieff is to be reduced to a commercial port. 4. Russia is to abandon her protectorate of the

Principalities, ft. Russia renounces certain territories in Bessarabia, which leaves the navigation of the Danube perfectly free. 6 A commission is to be appointed to trace the new frontiers in this district 7 The fact of a Russian soldier passing the Pruth is to lie lonk< d upon as a risns belli by the contracting Powers. " I believe this information is correct," says the Paris correspondent of the Post, " and to which might he added a revision of the Asiatic frontiers of Turkey, to accomplish which a commission will be also appointed.'' " It is affirmed," says the Patrie , that the " sub-committee appointed to draw up the text of the treaty of peace has not yet been able, notwithstanding all its exertions, to terminate its task. It is prop lble that the examination and approbation of this important document will necessitate several meetings of the Congress ; but the general belief is, that it can be signed and made public before the 31st of March, and that consequently the armistice need not be renewed." " Brother Jonathan." þÿ The origin of this term, as applied to the United States, is as follows : þÿ When General Washington, after being appointed commander of the army of the revolutionary war, went to Massachusetts to organise it, he found a great want of ammunition and other means for its defence ; and on one occasion it seemed that no means could be devised for the necessary safety Jonathan Turnbull, the elder, was then governor of the State of Connecticut ; and the General, placing the greatest reliance on his Excellency's judgment, remarked, " We must consult brother Jonathan on the subject." The General did so ; and the Governor was successful in supplying many of the wants of the army ; and thenceforth, when difficulties arose, and the army was spread over the country, it became a by-phrase, l< We must consult Brother Jonathan and the name has now become a designation for the whole country, ac John Bull has for England.

The Negro and the Needle. þÿ It is not generally known that, in the early progress of needle manufacture we are indebted to the negro. The earliest re cord of needlemaking in this country is in the year 1545, in the reign of Henry VIII., and it is supposed that this uspful branch of industry was introduced by a Moor from Spain. The historian Stowe tells us that needles were sold in Cheapside and other busy streets in London, in the reign of Queen Mary, and were at that time made by a Spanish negro, who refused to discover the secret of his art. Another authority states that the art of making steel needles was lost, at the negro's death, but was afterwards revived by a German in 1556. Probably these facts may account for the crest of the needlemakers' coat of arms being the head of a npgro.

Died in the night between the 25th and 26th inst. at his Estate Montpellier after a protracted and painful illness, in the 52nd a year of his age Carl Bithorn Esqr., native of Copenhagen, but since 1824 a resident of this Island. He has spent this long period of 32 years in various avocations and employments, and in them all, be they of a public or of a private nature, gained the esteem and good will of his fellow-citizens. He was for many years a useful and active member of the Burgher Council, and as a militia-officer his gentlemanly deportment and tact made him invariably beloved by all those whom he commanded, and it is a well-known fact that in the hour of danger not even the severest indisposition could prevent him from fulfilling his duty to its fullest extent, and it may with truth be said, that the firm decision evinced by him, blended as it was with considerate and humane mildness, has been of great service to this country. His numerous family loses the kindest husband and the tenderest father. His frie; dswill not forget, either the unswerving constancy of his affection and hospitality, or the unvarying liveliness of his animated and cheerful conversation, which no vicissitudes of life could affect or depress. Thus he will continue to live in the grateful and sorrowful remembrance of many : Peace be with his ashes ! þÿ Communicated.

C OIIj Iff U NIGAT E D þÿ THE DANISH LUTHERAN CHURCH. The Bazaar lately held for the repairs of this church, has as far as we are able to ascertain reached the amount of $1,400 þÿ this plainly shews the liberal and praiseworthy spirit of this community, as well as the generous feelings of absent friends who have also contributed liberally towards it. It might be adduced that this is quite natural, being the principal, and the Church of the State, that, to which the Government, Garrison and all public officers are attached, and whioh ought reasonably to be expected would be supported, and command the serious attention of the Authorities here, as well as those at Home þÿ but is it the case ? There is not a foreign congregation in the three Danish Islands but have each its own pastor, whereas in these three Islands in which there are seven lutheran congregations, there are never more than two, and for the last year but one clergyman to attend to them, can it therefore be wondered at the decline of the

Sunday Schools, and if one member of this church drops off after the other to attend other congregations, where divine service is regularly held every Sunday, whereas this church is only opened once a month for those attached to the Danish Congregation. It is now upwards of 9 months siDce the pastor of the St. Thomas Church died, yet we hear of no appointment of a new minister, the consequence of which is, that the Incumbent of this Island has been obliged to travel from one town to the other, and from Island to Island to perform divine service, which at the same time that this irregular service weans the members from their church, these frequent trips and multiplied vocations must harrass and unfit the Clergyman to perform his duties. Wherever the fault is to be laid, this appears certain : that the affairs of the Church are neglected, and is so much more to be regretted as the disposition of the Inhabitants in the present instance, as well as at St. Thomas when their lamented Pastor Tidemand died, have shewn how ready they are to contribute their mite for the benefit of the church when circumstances require it.

CLOSE OF THE PARIS CONFERENCES. PARIS, Friday Night. The Paris correspondent of the Morning Herald , says : þÿ issued, that the Emperor will hold a grand review of the army of Paris on Tuesday next, at 1 o'clock ; but the announcement of the review does not contain this most important and significant circumstance, that his Majesty will be accompanied by the Plenipotentiaries, whose work being done, they may enjoy the relaxation of the military spectacle, which in reality is ordered in their honour. There is no doubt that peace will be proclaimed at the latest on Monday. It is rumoured that the theatres will be opened gratis on that day, when cantatas will he sung, and odes recited, and peace welcomed, just as the birth of the Imperial heir had been on Monday week." It is expected that the signing of the treaty will be announced to the Parisian public by the firing of 100 guns. The tidings will be thus proclaimed before the Plenipotentiaries leave the Hall of Conferences, and the signatures are to be written with an Eagle's plume, which is to he richly mounted in jewellery, and preserved by the Empress Eugenie, who has expressed her particular desire to possess such a memorial of the restoration of peace. ft liBieft, The latest account from America puts the chances of our dispute in a new aspect. Walker, the filibuster, it should seem, has taken upon himself to interfere with the Nicaragua Transit Company, a concern protected under the Clayton-Bulwer treaty alike by Great

Britain and the United States. He has seized the Company's boats, annulled its charter, and granted a new one to another party. What makes all this the more eccentric is that he had refused the Presidency of Nicaragua even from his own party, and had ostensibly contented himself with remaining Generalin-Chief, so that his exercise of any authority over the concerns of such a body must be a palpable usurpation. AWFUL EARTHQUAKE AT JAPAN

The advices per the Baltic convey the intelligence of a dreadful earthquake, by which the town of Jeddo, in the island of Japan, was completely destroyed. The news was brought to San Francisco by the schooner Page, and the following are the particulars tOn the 11th of November, at 10 o'clock, p. m., a violent earthquake occurred at Jeddo,

, : þÿ s þÿ which destroyed 100,000 dwellings, 54 temples, and 30,000 inhabitants,. Fire broke out at the same time in 30 different parts of the city. The earth opened and closed over thousands of buildings, with their occupants. The shock was severe at Simoda. Although the distance from Jeddo to Simoda is but 60 miles, it appears that no official account of the earthquake had been received at the latter place at the time of the sailing of the schooner Page þÿ the 10th of December. The news was obtained through the Dutch interpreter. The Japanese seemed to attach little or no importance to the catastrophe. The inhabitants of the portion of the city destroyed were forewarned of the disaster, and many of thetn escaped. The buildings of Jeddo are chi.fl- if one story, and oourt.ueted of very Ugnt material. The temples of worship, however, are lofty, and in some instances are constructed of heavy masonry. Jeddo according to the best authorities, is the second capital of the empire, being tho residence of the military Emperor. It is located on the North-East coast of the island of Niphon, and contain a population of a million and a half of souls. It is stated to be enclosed by a trench, and intersected by numerous canals and branches of a river, navigable for vessels of a moderate burden. It has a fortified palace, with very extensive grounds, many noble residences profusely ornamented with sculpture and paintings, several large religious temples, and other publio edifices. It also contained the Imperial library,

composed of 150,000 volumes. The houses are mostly one story in height, but being generally built of wood, are subject to frequent destruction by fire ; certain it is that of the 100,000 dwellings demolished by the recent convulsion a large proportion of them fell a prey to the flames. Earthquakes are not unfrequent at Japan. We need scarcely refer to one in the bay of Simoda, a little more than a year ago, during which the Russian frigate Diana was wrecked. In 1596 a number of Japanese cities were destroyed and many thousand persons perished Indeed, that quarter of the globe has afforded the most extraordinary instances of the phenomenon on record. In 1663 an earthquake at Pekin buried 200,000 persons, and at the same place, about 70 years later, 100,000 were swallowed up.

EARTHQUAKE IN CALIFORNIA From the San Francisco Herald.) The severest shock of earthquake ever experienced in this vicinity since the settlement of California occurred on Friday morning, at just 24 minutes past 5 o'clock. Every building in this city and vicinity shook to its foundation, and in some quarters the houses swayed and rolled as vessels in a heavy sea. The inmates of every dwelling were awakened, and some were even thrown from their beds, so violent was the shock. Many persons rushed into the streets, and but that the circumstance of their sudden appearance was of a character to produce sensations of terror rather than merriment, the scene would have been most ludicrous. The large hotels were depopulated instanter, and in the general rush articles of furniture were thrown down, occasioning noises which added considerably to the clatter and confusion caused by the earthquake. Some estimate may be formed of the violence of the shock when it is stated that a man sleeping on the third floor of the Custom-house building was thrown from his bed to the floor. The walls of this building are composed of masonry capable of resisting a broadside from a ship of the line. Notwithstanding its immense bulk and strength, the building was tossed like a feather on the wave. The Monterey Sentinel of the 16th says: þÿ ' A hard shock of earthquake, coming apparently from the North-West, was felt in this town at 20 minutes past 6 o'clock vesterday morning."

I beg leave to address a few remarks to your readers, " Gracchi, in reference to the communications of the " which have appeared in the columns of your paper. " Anti-Gracchus" is correct in denying that any direct proposal has been made to the Colonics, offering to them the boon of self-government. So far true. He can, however, scarcely have the hardihood to deny that the question of selfgovernment is one which grows out of the agitated question of the future relation of the Colonies to Denmark. Both in the Diet, as well as in the Colonial Council, this question has led to the consideration of colonial self-government. True, it has only been viewed in the light of a future contingency ; which, sooner or later, it is foreseen, will force itself on the consideration of the mother-country and the Colonies. " In the other house of the Diet, the ' Landshis Speech to the Colonial Council " that the thing,' it was admitted," says the Governor in Law (regarding the relation of the Colonies to Denmark) had in its favor, that it created a certain colonial independence, thus however, that the Colonies for the first, should be subjected to a kind of guardianship on the part of the Diet." Whether the Colonies can, atany future time be better prepared for self-government, than they are now, is a question, in reference to which much may be said on both sides. The granting of colonial self-government, would, it appears to

me, give much ease to the Danish Ministry, which finds itself so perplexed by the question now brought before the Council, aud which gave rise to so much debate in the Diet, as to draw the admission from the Minister of the Interior, that it was found necessary to sacrifice the interests tional difficulty. þÿ of the Colonies to the settlement of a constitu- vide " Rigsdagstidende"No. 65. Truly an "unfortunate situation" as this Minister himself declared it to be. " Gracchus" is, no douht, mistaken in what he supposes to be an offer of self-government: still, in my humble opinion, it is now time that the Colonies should seek to have a greater participation in the direction of their affairs than before. When Ministers speak of a sacrifice of the Colonies, þÿ when in the regulation of our affairs that " I believe it is declared in the Diet, by one who has a voice the Colonies do not in any respect stand in such a relation to Denmark, that there can be a question of any great sympathy between them and us, as fellow-countrymen, or that in a national point of view, we can ascribe to them any considerable value." þÿ When these are the opinions held regarding us, we are fully justified, I think, in petitioning for the right to manage our own affairs. And what is there in the idea of self-government so repugnant to many ? Do we seek to establish independency? Do wc wish to sever the link which binds us to Denmark ? Far from it ! We wish simply to enjoy the benefit of a representative government.

" Who We hear the absurd question has been asked, are to be our Governors ?" A question easily þÿanswered Those whom Denmark appoints. The British Colonies are self-governed. The form of Government, in most cases being one divided into a Governor and Council elected by the Crown and a representative assembly elected by the People. All bills have the force of laws as soon as the Governor's assent is obtained, after having passed the Council and Assembly. The power of rejection is vested in the Crown, but, until rejected, the laws arc valid This brings ino to a consideration of the question, are we capable of self-government ? 1 can see no reason why we should not be. Our 1

3 £ 0 Us 0 I ATI a. I population mixed one, is a so is that of our neighbours the British W. 1. Colonies. We have a | unenlightened negro population, have so they. In whatever manner we endeavour to institute a comparison, we find a just one. Plain- I ly then, when a Mr. Lehman declares (and 1 suppose that he is not alone in this opinion) that he has no sympathy for us, we ought to have some for ourselves þÿ and as the only means of exercising it, we should endeavour a form of government, as will " save us from our to obtain such friends." In conclusion, I cannot but observe, that the manner in which the petition to the Colonial Council, praying for self-government, is being got up is very unsatisfactory and objectionable. Its object is not understood; and those opposed to every idea of self-government find it easy to misrepresent its character. A public meeting should have been convened : and, after a proper discussion on the matter, a petition should have been drawn up þÿ but not before. This would have corrected many false imprespure disinterestedness on the part of sions, and would have prevented an " exhibition of Anti-Gracchus." OBSERVER.

A Sicilian Prodigy. þÿ A letter from Naples says: þÿ Our attention has been a little divided of late between politics and a Sicilian child of ten years of age. An otficial note in the Court Journal, apprises the world that the King has been pleased to grant Girohamo di Majo, of Palermo, a pension of 4-50 ducats a year, until he has attained his 21st year. The reason assigned is, that " this child often years of age only, has shown hinislf to be possessed of varied knowledge and great sagacity of judgment, exquisite taste, and a fertile memory. The King, by such an assignment Cor the special education of this gifted child, has proved in what high consideration he holds intellectual culture, and how strongly lie desires, by every generous impulse, to contribute to its perfection and lustre !" The lad is acquainted with Greek, French, Spanish, and English ; all of which languages he translated freely into Italian, in your correspondent's rooms, taking for trial (lie Daily Netrs, the Greek Testament, Virgil, Horace, Scribe's Comedies ; and entering into conversation in French, English, and Spanish. The books were opened at hap-hazard. In history, whe-

ther English, Sicilian, or Roman history, it was impossible to puzzle him, and his answers were so far from being concisp that lie went on continuously from one fact to another, giving his opinions of their effects on the social condition of a people. His answers in geography, astronomy, and natural philosophy were not less correct and surprising, lie will work any sum in vulgar fractions, and with the Elements of Euclid is well acquainted. In fact, Girohamo di Majo is one of those splendid instances o( genius sometimes sent on earth, , as if to show how much higher destinies than the present await human nature, and to how much greater a height the human mind may obtain. All Naples, as well as Palermo, has seen him. Professor and prince, and foreign ministers, and last of all royalty, and all are alike astonished by this wonderful phenomenon. The lad will shortly return to complete his studies, under the guidance of the Benedictine monks of St. Martino, near Palermo.

LOCAL. A very daring act of theft was perpetrated in the town of Frederiksted on Friday night last. The Police Office was entered and an Ironchest, containing about twenty dollars and some Jewelry, extracted therefrom. It is supposed that the perpetrator or perpetrators made their ingress by the use of a false key, as neither the door nor the lock was broken. The Ironchest was found yesterday morning in an adjacent yard broken open þÿ the money and part of the jewelry were gone. While putting the above in type we learn that an attempt was made on Saturday night last to break into the lower story of Miss C. Rankin's house, in Princes Street, this town A movement upstairs at the time fortunately prevented the theft being committed. We hope that the guilty parties will be discovered and reoeive that punishment, which the law justly deals out to such offenders

We have been kindly favored with the loan of the following letter, which treats of a new meby the use of " convex and concave perforated thod of burning wet megass and other damp fuel grating bars." We alluded to the subject in the month of July last, and beg again to direct the attention of the Planters in this Island to it : þÿ " Port of Spain, Trinidad, > May 10, 1S56. ) F. Beichman Esqr. Danish Consul, Trinidad. Sir ! quiries concerning my " convex and con- I have the honour to reply to your incave grating bars." The bars are hollow, and perforated, so that the air becomes slightly heated before it is mixed with the tlames. The use of these bars are to burn damp or wet megass, sawdust, and other kinds o.' fuel which could not be used with the present or common grating bars. As it was rather late in the season when I obtained my patent here, and the new moulds and castings taking a considerable time to complete 1 have as yet only set up Two complete sets, one for the Colonial government here, and another on a large estate under a boiler which works a steam still. The manager certifies that he produces more steam than he could obtain before and that he uses wet megass direct from the mill ; the bars answering beyond his expectations. Those which are used at the government sawmill under my own care burn sawdust, chips, and mineral pitch, requiring hardly any fuel besides the waste or offal of the timber sawn. Neither sawdust nor chips from the plaining machine could be used as a fuel with

the common grating bars. As a strong draft is required when burning wet megass or other wet fuel, chimneys ought to be from 65 to 80 feet high. The cost of a set of my convex and con- " cave perforated grating bars" is from 70 to 80 dollars and the license for the use of them is 25 dollars for 2 years. The cost price can be reduced in case large quantities are wanted, when it will become more economical to have them cast in the United States. Iron castings here are charged at the rate of 10 cents per pound. As they require very little alterat.ons in the fire places one or two days are sufficient to take out the common grating bars and to insert those constructed on my plan. I)ANL. B. KEATING."

A New Religious Order. þÿ A correspondent of the Independence Beige writes from Rome, that a meeting of prelates just held at Loretto, under the presidency of the Cardinal De Angelis, it was resolved to establish in each of their respective dioceses a society of Sacconi, so called from their wearing a dress in the form of a sack, with a hood ; and also a cord round the loins, sandals on their feet, and a veil, pierced with two holes for the eyes, over the face. The correspondent adds, þÿ " These religieux, janissaries of the holy office, are to have the task of penetrating all kitchens on Fridays, peeping into pots, stewpans, and porridge-basins; to ascertain whether the prescriptions for the soup are being transgressed ; and are also to rummage amongst the papers to discover any trace of impiety or revolution. They will have to denounce the blasphemers and a portion of the fine is promised to them for this. At eight o'clock in the evening, when the hell announces the Angelus, the Sacconi will take note of all who omit to kneel even in the street ; and will denounce all such. These regulations, and some others, have been issued in a printed form from the episcopal printing-office of Fermo."

j KUROPE A N. THE ITALIAN QUESTION. A Genoa paper lately announced a political amnesty as imminent in Naples. Tbe Paris I'm-

priest-ridden couutry more authentic than that of the Italian paper, indignantly repels the calumny on king Bute ha, and denies that there is the least pretence for affirming that lie is about ! to lay aside or soften the terrors of his venj gcancc. The Risorgimcvto of Turin, after stating that the resignation Foreign Affairs, has been accepted, and that Count di Cavour lias been provisionally intrusted with that portfolio, adds that this resignation has no political meaning; that General de la Marmora having returned, the portfolio of War will he restored to him, and that the present Minister of War, General Durando, will resume the portfolio of Foreign Affairs. The Risorgimcntn of the 2nd of May says: þÿ The note, or, to give it the true name, the protest, which Count Cavour, in the name of the Piedmontcse Government, sent to the represen- | tatives of the different Powers before quitting Paris, will soon he published. It insists, in lu.tr- | guage always becoming, but firm and energetic, on I the necessity of providing efficaciously for the welfare of Italy, if they truly desire the tranquility of Europe. The state of siege in the duohies, the military government in Lombardy, the Austrian garrisons in Tuscany, ,the foreign occupation in the Rotnagna, the over-crowded prisons of Naples and Sicily þÿ all constitute a slate of things not natural, and which cannot last. The . Congress of Paris lias recognised the misfor- tunes of Italy, and in that European Congress

the right of Piedmont to speak for Italy has been recognised. The following telegraphic report of what took place in the Sardinian Chamber on Tuesday last appears in the Independance tietge of Wednesday : þÿ Turin, May 6. Count Cavour, in answer to interpellations addressed to him to-day in the Chamber of Deputies declared that the negotiations now pending on the subject of the affairs of Italy imposed upou hitn a great reserve. He explained the moral and material advantages arising out of the Treaty of Peace. The Italian question has been brought before the Congress, and France and England have frankly adopted the views of Piedmont. Austria had met the question hy a plea of not discussiug it, hut the Italian question has not the less become now a European question. The Minister declared, in conclusion, that tlio relations between Sardinia and Austria had not improved. The Piedtnontese government placed its solo reliance on the omnipotence of public opinion.

From the St. Thomas Times, May 31 DEMUR ARA. SUPREME COURT OF CRIMINAL JUSTICE SENTENCE OF .tOltN SAYERS ORR Monday, April cs. His Honor the Chief J itdgc having summed up the case, addressed the prisoner in the following language " I think you have adopted the wisest course : þÿ You have been found guilty of a misdemeanor, that is, of having unlawfully met and assembled with divers persons unknown for the purpose of stirring up jealousies among the inhabitants, and especially to promote among the native black and coloured inhabitants feelings of hostility against the Portuguese residents ; atul with having, while so assembled and gathered together, armed with sticks, staves, and other offensive weapons, and during all that time using violent and unlawful speeches, endeavoured to stir up jealousies The trial has lasted very long, and the jury have been very patient, and my charge would have been very much longer hut I nut I saw at once that they were weary of hearing the same thing gone over again and again. 1 felt convinced that they were themselves men of clear understanding and comprehension enough to understand the case and make up their minds, and that nothing that fell from me could alter their opinion. Besides, it isn.it my duty to alter their opinions, but to lead them to a fair and unbiassed decision. That decision lias been given, and it cannot be said that the decision has been biassed by any thing that I urged upon them. Thus, you have convicted by a jury of your own countrymen; for

break- j your boast is that yon belong to this country. It gives me great pain to seo a man of intellect, and who would he a matt of high intelligence, if Ins intellect was properly directed, leading the ignorant and I uninformed into courses sttclt as you have led them into. There is no palliation for your conduct, and although I am not preaching to you, and I pray you not to take it in that light, I iuipe you have seen that the law is able to protect the right and punish the wrong. It is a most ridiculous and absurd idea, that the soil of this country, which belongs to the Queen, belongs to the Creoles. Nobody can deny that vers , professing to Itave intelligence regarding the i that is the idea that has got abroad. It is folly to shut one's eyes to it. It is necessary to set ourselves against it, and those who will tint be restrained must he restrained by tbe strong arm of the law. Tbe sentence upon you is, that you be imprisoned in one ot Her Majesty's jails for the term of three years, and and kept to hard labour during such imprisonment Further, that whenever you shall be discharged, you shall enter into security lor keeping the peace, your of Chevalier Cibrario, Minister of | self in 11300, and two sureties m £150 each."

SPEECH OF HIS EXCELLENCY GOVERNOR SCI1LEGEL INTROIM'CTORY TO THE DRAFT OF A I. AW REGARD. ISO THE REGULATION OF THE POSITION OF DEN- MAKE TO THE DANISH WEST INDIES. DELIVERED AT THK 6TH MEETING OE THE THIRD SESSION OE THE COLONIAL COUNCIL, THURSDAY, HT1I OF MAY. ISM.) " In virtue of a most gracious order of II. M. the King I have the honor to lay before the honorable Assembly the Draft of a Law alluded to by me at the opening of the session, regarding the regulation of the position of the Danish Monarchy and of the Kingdom of Denmar . to the Colony in the West Indies.

only on account of its pre-eminent importance beyond any Law that up to the present has been submitted to the discussion of the Assembly, but also with respect to the form in which it is produced. It has not been framed by Ministry, the but it is the result of a discussion which took place in the " Folkething," the one of the two other House, the " Landsthing," and been Houses of the Diet, has been acceded to the adopted by the Ministry, which has declared its intention of making it the basis of ulterior debates in the Legislative Assembly for the entire Monarchy. " In order to enable the honorable members front the very commencement to view the Draft in the right light, I will premise a remark, to which I shall have to revert again at a later stage of my explanations : It is not our task, on a free basis to lay down new rules for the position of the Colony to the Mother-Country, but to solve questions which have arisen from the alterations that have taken place in the constitutional relations of the latter. A Fundamental Law for tho entire Danish Monarchy has been promulgated the 2nd October 1855, and the Fundamental Law for Denmark of the year 1849, to the sphere of which, as defiued in 2 of the Colonial Law of the 26th March 1852, the Colony has hitherto belonged, has been limited to the separate affairs of Denmark proper. The interior affairs of the Colony have been classed among the latter, consequently in a constitutional sense they continue to belong to the province of the Danish Diet.

The question actually at issue is therefore : which affairs are interior affairs , and , what effect and extent is to be given to a division of the colonial affairs into interior affairs under the Funda-
Croix Avis AF ENK E-M ADAME HARRIET CHKISTIAMSTIOII, TIRKDAttEM, Hen lOile .11 AI. IS16.

mental Law of 1849, and not interior affairs under the General Constitution of the 2nd October 1855 ? " A further consequence of the peculiar nature j of this Law Draft is, that it is laid before the j honorable Assembly unaccompanied by any explanations. The ideas and considerations, on | which it is based, may be learnt from the debates ! of the Diet, of which a few copies will be laid on the table for the use of the honorable Assembly. ! They are so extensive, our time and the forces | at our command are so circumscribed, that not even the translation of a part of them could be effected : only the Dratt itself with tho explanations with which it was laid before the Diet by the Ministry have been translated. Some of the honorable members will by this want of translai tion be prevented from making themselves acquainted with the documents thus exhibited, ac- 1 have therefore found myself called upon to j company the Draft with a succinct exposition of the circumstances, which have called it forth and ; of the discussions to which it has given rise. " The Committee which in all probability will : be appointed to prepare this matter in the As- | sembly might possibly, and may even after the but will be delivered at the rate of 6 cents ! explanations I am about to offer, find it advisable | to attach to their Report a similar exposition ; I nevertheless I thought, that it might have some interest for those members to whom the riocu- I inents in question from linguistic reasons are in-

accessible, already now to be enabled to form a | general conception of the questions here at stake, i 1 will merely add, that I am going to give nothing ; hut an historical Report, abstaining from all reflections on tho substance of the matter itself, which could possibly be interpreted as intended to influence the honorable Assembly in one di- ! rcction or the other. " It is well known to the honorable members that the principle of legislation, administration and finance of the Colony, under the old consti- ; tution of tho Danish State was, as pronounced by the Ordinance of the 31st March 1755, that the Danish should be the Law of the Lard through- out these Islands þÿ " as far as it might be applicable," adds the Royal Rescript of the 22nd September 1758. A more recent Royal Resolution, of the 6th June 1821, has laid down the rule : that it in every individual case should bo " This Law Draft is of a peculiar nature, not decided, whether and how far a legal enactment promulgated for Denmark was to be extended to the Colony, whilst of course at the same time sundry special laws have been issued for the Islands, without however affecting the general character of their legislation as originally and materially Danish. The Danish Supreme Court is, as we all know, also the highest and last tribunal for the dijudicature of West India lawsuits. The legal systems valid in other parts of the Monarchy have never had either practical force or influence in the Colony. " The administration as well as the framing of

Laws were partly committed to the same Authority to which in Denmark the direction of the Departments of Justice, Police, in Church and Schools and the civil legislation general was delegated, viz., the Royal Board of Justice it and Home Department, (Chancery) ; partly was given over to the Board of Trade and Customs, which was intrusted with the Departments ot Commerce, Navigation, Industry and Manufactures for the entire realm, as also with the Finances of the Colonies, in fact, with all matters exclusively colonial In regard to the finances, which, as I have mentioned just now, belonged entirely to the province of the Board of Trade and Customs, it was the rule which in substance as yet remains unaltered, that the West India Treasury formed a part of the general State Treasury, into which any surplus of revenue was to flow and by which any under-balance would have to be covered, the Colonial Budgets and Accounts to form parts of the general State Budgets and State Accounts " The first alteration in this system was effeoted in the year 1848. By a Royal Resolution of the 18th August the same which contains the first

Mr. 47. enactments bearing upon the Emancipation that had taken place in the Islands þÿ it was, with a view of concentrating the Colonial Administration, ordained : that the Ministry of Commerce (which had succeeded to the Board of Trade and Customs) was to revise all Reports aud Propositions, to whichever branch of the Administration they might belong, from the Colonial Government, the same however not to propose or to decide upon anything without having previously conferred on the matter with the Ministry to the province of which it might appertain. In the mean time the Fundamental Law of Denmark which substituted the constitutional for the absolute form of Monarchial Government, was proclaimed on the 5th June 1849. In regard to the effects exercised by this event on the Colony, I can refer to the introductory wcrds of the explanations with which the Minister of Finances accompanied the Draft of the Colonial Law, laid before the Diet in the year 1851 : " ' Whereas it must appear unquestionable, that tho Fundamental Law of Denmark also comprises the West India Colony as an annex of the Mother Country, and in particular, that it entails an equal responsibility upon the Minister intrusted with the colonial affairs, and that it therefore would be perfectly irrational to think of retaining the absolute form of Government solely for the Danish West India Possessions, it was on the other hand, as has also been acknowledged in the debates of the Legislative Diet, a supposition necessitated by the particular that nature of the practical relations in question, the

Fundamental Law could not conveniently, in a direct manner be promulgated in those Possessions, and it was therefore that the Council of State, when the Fundamental Law had emanated in the year 1 849, resolved that it should not be published there, and consequently not with all its specified enactments be put in force in the said Possessions. Nevertheless, the effects of the Fundamental Law will indirectly as well as directly extend to the Colonies, and the notion of the highest legislative power of the realm involves in itself, that it must to a comprehensive and unlimited degree be applicable to all the Colonial Possessions attached to the Empire.' " I presume that these words will suffice to make clear to the honorable Assembly the views which at that time in His Majesty's Ministry prevailed in regard to the position of the cause to the Mother Country, 1 shall however Colony a copy of these explanations to be laid on the table for the information of the honorable Council. To t/ie Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir, Having heard some remarks regarding the non-appearance of the Proceedings of the Colonial Council in the Avis, I beg to call your attention to the matter; as it is presumed, that the subscribers of the present day have the same claim as those of former days, who through the medium of the newspaper were furnished with the proceedings of the Council. I am Sir, Your obdt. Servant, June 6th 1856.
THE 15 "AVIS." a "i Christiansted, St. Croix. þÿ TUESDAY , 10 th JUNE , 1856

VVe adverted to a communication from " X" in our last issue, which article appears in our columns to-day, and in answer to it wo must observe, that, to the best of our knowledge, the larger portion of our Subscribers are more satisfied to see other matter, than the proceedings of the Colonial Council inserted in our paper. This preference arises from the meagerness of the report of the debates as furnished by the Colonial Council. Far from its being interesting, we have heard complaints in reference to its conciseness, which, it was said, amounted to unintelligibility. Let it not be supposed, that our subscribers of former days were furnished with these proceedings by us from choice. We were then compelled, without payment, not only to insert them in Danish and English, but also to insert Drafts of Laws &c. in both languages. a large number of our Subscribers, after complaining that our paper was for months filled with such matter, withdrew their subscription. Now, when from the impossibility of longer carrying on the establishment on such a principle, we are paid for advertisements &c., the choice is, of course, left lo us whether we will insert these proceedings or not. The latter course we adopt from the reasons above mentioned. No one can be more interested in the perusal of the proceedings of public bodies than we are, but then we expect an intelligible report of those proceedings. We are perfectly willing, at our own expense, to send a reporter to the Colonial Council, to report for our

paper : but this privilege we are denied ; and instead of whatever pleases the Colonial Council dry thereof we are furnished with a concise and to make report public. Still we will abide by the decision of our Subscribers. If two-thirds of the number request us to insert the proceedings in question as furnished by the Colonial Council, we will they willingly are do so, and feel pleasure in the act. But until then, we give the Colonial Council all the benefit which it desires from the non-publicity of its meetings.
EUROPEAN EXTRACTS. AUSTRIA. The Times correspondent at Vienna, writes as follows, dated May 10: " Qn

the 8tli i n st. tlie representatives of Austria and Prussia officially informed the German Diet that peace was restored, and at the same time proposed that the Bund should express its adhesion to the treaty of peace concluded at Paris on the 30lh of March. It is well known that the Confederation intends to express its approval of the policy of the two great German Powers, hut it would have been a sacrifice of dignity to dispose of the matter, brevi manit, and, therefore, at the demand of Bavaria, it was referred to the Committee on Eastern affairs. In political circles it is related that the aforesaid committee will propose that the Bund return to Austria and Prussia its thanks for their defence of the interests of Germany at Paris, and also express its entire approbation of their policy in the Eastern question. The adhesion of the German Diet to the treaty of March 30 is a matter of little importance to the Western Powers, but it certainly is a great triumph for this Government, which for nearly three years in vain endeavoured to obtain from its federal allies an unqualified approval of its policy. The Austrian public is at present so greatly occupied with internal affairs that the Eastern question has ceased to he a topic of conversation. The Concordat, the various industrial undertakings, the dissensions between Barons Bach and Bruck, and the appointment of Baron Hubner to he the representative of his Imperial Royal Apostolic Majesty at the French Court, are now

the exclusive objects of conversation. The aristocracy did not condescend lo trouble itself about Baron llubner as long as lie was merely the diplomatic agent of the Austrian Government ; hut it openly expresses its disbelief that a plebeian by birth can worthily represent the sacred person of the Emperor. His Majesty, however, is of a different opinion ; tor he, a few days since, definitively appointed Baron" lluhner to lie his Ambassador at Paris. The heaw charge brought by the proud Vienna dames against the diplomatist is, that he is "a glazier's son," and tliey, one and all, vow that, when he returns to Vienna, they will not admit him to their drawing-rooms. Such a threat may appear a matter of singularly little import ance to persons who are not initiated into the mysteries of high life in Vienna, hut those who are, will well know what Baron Hubner's position is likely to he. It was long ago whispered that "the ministers ot the Home Department and of Finances did not work well together, daggers drawn " Both Baron Bach and hut it is now affirmed that they are "at Baron Bruck stand high in the favour of their Sovereign, hut they are both very ambitious men, and consequently extremely jealous of each other's influence. I he so-called well-informed public thinks that the conflict will end by the dismissal of one or other of the ministers, but, lor reasons which will he given, such is not my opinion. Baron Bach, who is, perhaps, the fittest man in the empire for the post which he

occupies, has the support of the Church party, while Baron Bruck has the sup port of the financial world. If Baron Bach quitted office, the papal chair wonld lose one of its most trusty friends in Austria ; and if Baron Bruck resigned his portfolio, the premium on the precious metals would, in a very few days, be as high as it was a few months since. The Minister of Finance has fewer enemies thau the Minister of Home Depart ment, but the latter has perhaps more influential friends.

THE MISSING STEAMER PACIFIC. The following is an extract of a letter just received by a clergyman in this country from a friend of his in New York, who sailed from Liverpool in the Atlantic on the 6th of February, that port: þÿ 14 days after the Pacific had started from " New York, February 26th 1856. Eighteen weary disagreable stormy days brought us on Sunday morning to New York. The captain, who had crossed the Atlantic 243 times, declared he had never had such a bad trip as this. The ship had scarcely got out of the Mersey when the head wind began increasing to a

gale, against which When reached this shore. we had to fight until we two days out the fog became so thick that we could not see the length of the vessel On the third day the floating ice began to make its appearance, increasing to such an extent that we could only feel our way. For captain two days Fog, fog, fog nothing hoping and ! nights kept crawling moment, to get we out but of fog it and every ice along, ! On the the j third day, at 7 o'clock in the morning, we saw a spectacle which none on board will ever forget ; it was in fact the finger of Providence, and some more deserving than I and others must have been onboard. The whole veil of fog rose like a curtain, and we looked upon an ocean scene beautiful, fearful and grand. The atmosphere, as far the eye could reach was clear ; the sun shone brightly on a continuous chain of icebergs above 100 feet high, intermingled with the fields of and ice. the Chain after chain burst upon sight, sight was awfully impressive. In a less time than it has taken to write this, the curtain descended, and all became obscurity again The captain took the hint, and turned his ship towards England for the remainder of the day, and towards the South at night not resuming his course to America until the following morning After 18 days' passage, we arrived at New York, when we learnt that the Pacific, another steamer belonging to this, which sailed 14 days before us, had not arrived and I fear she is lost, with all cn board Our ship behaved nobly ; nothing broken or strained. It is won-
derful how man combines wood and iron to withstand the power of the waves."
(From the Illustrated London News, March 29.) THE BALTIC FLEET.

A fleet of screw gun-boats nearly 100 in number, is now in commission at Motherbank, of which each is of sixty-horse power, and aver- age nine knots an hour. These " hornets" are ariued with 68 and 32 pounder pivet-guns, and 24-pounder brass howitzers. The three principal divisions belonging to the divisional ships (Algiers, 91, Captain Codrington ; Colossus, 81, Captain Keppel ; and Brunswick , 81, Captain Yelverton) have their mastheads respectively painted red, white, and blue. The possession of this terrific force cannot be too highly estimated No line-of-battle ship could be safe at 1000 yards range, and, owing to their light draught of water (four and six feet), they could force their passage-through the most shallow of the enemy's creeks ; besides which their 68-pound shells would tell at -1000 yards upon a ship or arsenal There are, at the least another hundred all but completed, and about to be commissioned, the whole of which will be reviewed in connection with liners and frigates, at Spithead, by her Majesty on or about the 10th April. There will be also at that period a new description of scrcw-gun dispatch-vessels, equally elegant and powerful. These beautiful specimens of British naval architecture have been built in the Government and private yards; they will average a speed of sixteen knots an hour, and will mount five of the heaviest pivotguns. In addition to these there will be 100 iron and wood mortar-vessels of the most powerful build, each armed with a 13-inch mortar,

weighing five tons, besides half-a-dozen mortarfrigates (old 42s. converted). To sum up, then, England is prepared with þÿ Line-of-battle ships .42 Heavy frigates 56 Corvettes 123 Gun-boats 220 Mortar- vessels 100 Troop-frigates 10 Transports 340
Total 891 And nearly the whole of this gigantic force is composed of screw or paddle-box ships, besides an immense reserve. Well may Russia be desirous of coming to terms !

M. Kossuth on the Austrian Concordat. þÿ On Wednesday evening M. Kossuth delivered the first of two lectures, at the Spafields Schoolroom, " Concordat Exmouth-street, Clerkenwell, on the between the Pope and Francis Joseph of Austria, with special reference to Hungary in general, and the Protestantism of Hungary in particular." The charges for admission were 2s. and Is., and the spacious room was crowded; the Rev. Mr. Thoresby" presiding. M.

ST ® & £/ I ii T I 3 Kossuth, who was received with- loud cheers, remarked that the Concordat was, on the part of the Pope, a daring and dangerous manifestation of aspiration to universal supremacy, and, on the part of the Austrian Emperor, a shameful surrender of the most sacred rights of the crown, the clergy, and the people. To Hungary the consequences would be very serious. That country had been chosen as the field for this aggression because she was disarmed and helpless ; but he hoped the time would come when Providence would afford her the means of shaking off the fetters of tyrauny and oppression. Iu conclusion, M. Kossuth pointed out the troubles which the triumph of the Concordat in Hungary might in time bring upon England, and quoted a remark made upon the subject by Oliver Cromwell in 1688. The meeting separated with three cheers for the lecturer. The European journals express divers opinions on the all-absorbing topic, peace ; and we think we are warranted in regarding them only as conjectures, in the absence of any official notice of the conditions or terms of the treaty of peace. An Imperial Manifesto, of which we subjoin an extract, shews how the Czar lias tried to make the best of a bad bargain, while the declaration of peace was hailed with demonstrations of great joy by the Russian populace. The subjoined extracts will enable our readers to judge for themselves.

Latest Intelligence ! RUSSIA. The Imperial Manifesto. þÿ The following is an extract from the Imperial Manifesto, published at St. Petersburg on the 1st of April, to an- nounce the signing of the treaty of peace : " The obstinate and suDguinarv struggle which, for

nearly three years, has subverted Europe, has at last ceased. It was not Russia that commenced it. Even before it broke out my late august father, of imperishable memory, solemnly declared to his faithful subjects, and to all the foreign Powers, that the sole object of his desires and of his efforts had been to protect the rights of our co-religionists in the East, and to put an end to the persecutions to which they were subjected. Russians ! your efforts and your sacrifices have not been in vain. A great work has been accomplished, although by other and unforeseen means, and we may now with a quiet conscience put an end to those efforts and to those sacrifices by restoring to our dear country the inestimable blessings of peace. To hasten the conclusion of the treaty of peace, and to dispel, even for the future, the very idea of ambitious views or projects which might be attributed to us, we have consented to the adoptiou of certain precautionary measures, ij-c. These concessions are not great when put in comparison with the charges of a prolonged war, and the advantages promised to us by the tranquility of the Empire, the destinies of which it has pleased God to entrust to us. May all those advantages be obtained by our efforts, united to those of all our faithful subjects." þÿ Picture Times. The Russian Minister of Finance notified on the 5th instant, at St. Petersburg, that a treaty of peace having being signed, the merchant-vessels of the Western Powers will be admitted to Russian ports.
The number of armed vessels which Russia and Turkey are to have in the Black Sea, for the purpose of police and defence of the coasts is not to exceed ten for each Power.

(From the Illustrated Loudon News, April 5.) FRANCE, Paris, Thursday. Nothing but rejoicings are, as may be supposed, the order ot the day ; fetes and illuminations succeed without intermission ; on Tuesday took place the most magnificent review that has been seen for many a day in this country, where military spectacles are so much in the habits and tastes of all classes Upwards of 150.000 men took part in this review ; besides all the troops in garrison in Paris, nearly all those within some days' inarch of the capital were called upon to attend, and all the villages, as far as the department of Seine and Oise, were disposed so as to receive the arrivals, during at least four days. A brilliant sunshine, a cloudless sky, and a temperature greatly softened from the rigour of the keen east winds, that prevailed nearly all last month, gave everything that was requisite to complete the splendour and effect of the spectacle, which afforded to the many foreigners present on the occasion a good idea of the resources of a nation which, without having had breathingtime allowed it from the termination of such a campaign, could produce a similar spectacle.

CONCLUSION OF A MARITIME ARMISTICE. The Moniteur of Sunday published the following announcement : þÿ " Awaiting the ratification of the treaty of peace, a maritime armistice has been concluded between France, Great Britain, Sardinia and Turkey on the one hand, and Russia on the other; it has consequently been agreed that the prizes made after the signature of the treaty shall be restored ; that orders shall be issued for the immediate raising of existing blockades, and that the prohibitive measures taken in Russia against the exportation during the war of Russian produce, and especially that of corn, shall be likewise repealed without delay. The consular duties and requisite formalities as regards shippers and traders will be provisionally performed by the agents of the Powers who consented during the war to take charge ofjicieusement of the interests of the subjects of the belligerent States."

The Journal des Debals of Monday contains a very long article treating of the mode in which the Congress has disposed of the Fifth Article, the one allowing to the belligerent Powers the right to produce special conditions in a European interest The Russian Plenipotentiaries, it said, made no opposition to the demands following as the natural consequnce of the neutralization of the Black Sea. They did not defend either the military arsenal of Nicolaieff, or their naval establisments in the Black Sea or upon the shores of the Black Sea, in the Sea of Azoff, or upon the shores of the Sea of Azoff. The treaty of peace proclaims in the widest and most absolute sense the principle of the neutralization of these two seas. Henceforth they will simply be commercial seas, open to all vessels of commerce, closed to all those of war. The Russian ports and cities will be accessible to all Governments, who will beable to exercise an active surveillance by means of consular agents. All the Russian forts which are constructed upon the shores of the Black Sea, along the Caucasus until the last extremety of the Russian territory, not far from Batoum, will be destroyed, and cannot be replaced. With regard to the Russian fortresses upon the Southern side of the Caucasus, from the Black Sea to the Caspian, the allies have given way; but the treaty provides that the frontier which separates Russia and Turkey at this part shall be rectified, and that the Russians shall abandon their conquests and return from Kars

into their own territory Russia lireserves its possession ot the Aland Isles, only on the condition never to fortify them, or maintain there a military position. This stipulation is considered | very favourable to Sweden ; Stockholm the Empress, desiring to connect this great oc- i being but three or four hours' distance by steamer from those islands. The treaty pronounces the suppression of the Russian protectorate in the Danubian Principalities, but the Conference still hesitates between the different systems of political and administrative organisation which have been proposed.

THE PANURIAN PRINCIPALITIES. With regard to the future organisation of the Principalities, the Dcbats, in a recent article, states: " The Conference has the intention, it is said, of selecting from its body three commissioners, who will be sent to the spot to make inquiries

and report to Paris the result of their information and their personal impressions. Such a mission would demand much time, and might delay the closing of the labours of the Congress. This would be only a light inconveuience ; it would be more grave were the faith of the com- I missioners to be shaken þÿ were their conclusions to be denied, or the authority of the decisions of I the Conference to be disturbed by new and unexpected events. This has often been the case ; the Congress of Vienna committed more than one error, it decreed more than one measure which was never executed, more than one law which I nations either disdained or abrogated. The Conference has not yet chosen its commissioners, and their choice appears to be another source of hesitation ; for it will be necessary that the three I persons chosen should inspire an equal confidence in all classes of the Moldavian and Wallachian populations. The Plenipotentiaries of Austria, Russia, and Turkey are probably those who are I j best acquainted with the state of the provinces, ' their wishes, wants, and interests ;' but could it be asked of them to inquire and report on the civil and military acts of administration which have emanated from the Governments they represent ? Would it not be to ask them, in a certain manner, to report against themselves ? We have done nothing more than indicate the difficulties of the question." The same journal thus alludes to the continued occupation " The presence of the Principalities by Austria : of that Austrian army will give

rise to the just protest of Russia, and it will be necessary to avoid giving birth to new subjects of quarrel in that part of Europe. It is assured that all these questions have Dot been solved by the treaty of peace, and have not ceased to be the objects of the deliberation of the Conference."

the first place, our Transatlantic, relatives þÿ even those who talk most loudly and illogiþÿcall) upon the subject þÿ do not, and never did, mean to go to war with us, either on account of the Foreign Enlistment Bill or on that of the Central American dispute. In the second place, the persons whose angry words reach us from the other side of the ocean do not speak for the American people, but for a small section of them. In the third place, supposing all the bluster of t he Ami-Anglian faction to have meant something, and to have been adopied in iis spirit and its consequences by the Government of the United Slates, the circumstances of Europe, and of Great Britain more particularly, have changed so greatly since the conclusion of peace with Russia, that those who might not have hesitated to provoke this country six months ago would certainly hesitate to do so at the present lime. We dismiss altogether ihe Enlistment

it has already received. That ol Central America is more complicated. On the fiist question i tie British Government has yielded þÿ because it was in the wrong. On the only i second question it will not, dare not, and because it is in Ihe right; and because a principle is involved, the pusillanimous betrayal of which would impair the dignity and tarnish the honour of this nation. The Americans, with a not unnatural desire to extend their dominion over the North American continent, have quarrelled from time to lime with Mexico, and have managed by diplomacy, or by war, or by shutting their eyes to the doings of Filibusters and t outlaws, to annex large and valuable territories to the States. Theii doing so is no business of ours. This country does not seek to intermeddle in the wars of the Wesiern Hemisphere ; but if the Government of the United States, cither from a mania for

annexation, or from a tolerance for the proceedings of Filibusters, should attack the rights of ihis country, in Canada, New Brunswick, Newfoundland, nr Mosquitia, or suffer its subjects to do so, without affording tedress the mutter assumes another aspect. The United States have permitted American citizens to invade Nicaragua ; and Great Britain neither complains, nor asserts any right to complain, or even to remonstrate. The Governor of Nicaiagua issued a proclamation no the St h of (February last annexing to Nicaragua þÿ which on its side is evidently preparing tor ils own annexation to the United States þÿ a portion, if not the whole, of the territory of Mosquitia. By this act the rights of England are directly invaded. Mosquitia is tinder the protection of this country, a ad has been so since the year 1687, when the: then King made a formal and voluntary cession of his dominions to Great Britain ; which, without occupying his country, bound heiself to protect him and his successors.. This right was respected even by the Spamiards. at a time when they claimed, as the Americans appear to do now, to he lords paramount of the soil ot Geniral America. Those Americans who would annex Mosquitia, and who endeavour to justify the acts of the Governor ol Nicaragua' assert thiit. by the treaty known as Ihe Clayj ton-Bulwer treaty. Great Britain renounced her sovereignly over that district. The American difficulties will blow þÿover- In I British Government denies that it ever did

make such renunciation ; that it ever intended to make renunciation ; and maintains that neither the words of the treaty, nor ils spirit and obvious nveaning. hear out in the remotest degree the- interpietation sought to be put upon them. Great Britain has offered to submit the dispute to aibitration, and to abide by the uvrard ; and the United þÿStates Government has threateued to refuse arbitration, and to submit the dispute, if need he, to the decision of the sword. We believe the threat to be a a idle one. We do not believe that any Government will so dare to set the public opinion of its own people and that of the world at defiance. But, in order to be prepared for all conlingencus. the British and French Governments, al ihe request of the British and French residents in IVlosquitia, have resolved to unite their naval foices now in the Mexican Gulf, and dispatch them immediately for the protection ol Greytown. There is a. disposition on the part of some members of ihe United þÿStales Government to disavow the proceedings ol the Filibusters in and out of office in Nicaragua. We are glad to observe this, for it shows teturning reason, or at the least a misgiving that such a course will ullimaiely become imperative Indeed, President Fierce himself appears lo have taken preliminary steps towards escaping from the dilemma into which he has drifted, and speaks in his recent Message to Congress of lawless þÿproceedings that must be those of General Walker and the other Americans who have thrust the Union

into this perplexity. Let us hope that this disposition on the part of the American Government will grow powerful enough io dictate the policy of the Union. PROTECTION TO WOMEN Sir E. þÿPerry M s otion. The following petition, which has already received more than 1500 signatures of both in Liverpool, will shortly be sent up to Mr. Joseph C. Ewart for presentation to the House of Commons: þÿ To the Honourable the House of Commons of of Great Britain and Ireland , in Parliament assembled, the petition of the Lndersigned Inhabitants of Liverpool, Humbly Sheweth, That vour Petitioners fully recognize those essential principles of all civilised society-personal property ; which give to all its members freedom liberty and of the action, rights and of security in the inviolable possession of the fruits of their ndustry. That the existing law of this country, which gives to the husband, under ordinary circumstances, the entire control over the wife's property and earnings, is a violation of those principles, and is manifestly unjust. That the power thus conferred upon the husband is freqently abused by the selfish and profligate ; the law thus tacitly encouraging that violence and brutality which is of bo frequent occurrence, and which is such a disgrace to our age and country. That, by the operation or silence of the law, the power of the industrious and prudent wife to support and educate her children, when thoso duties are neglected by the idle and dissolute husband, is seriously impaired, or rendered impossible ; thus extending the injury BUBtained by the wife to the hapless children, who are too often brought up in pauperism, ignorance and crime.

That the law with respect to settlements and trusteeships, by which women possessing property, can in some cases imperfectly protect themselves, is too complicated and expensive to be available to the poor, for whose earnings the law provides no protection, and upon whom the evil falls in unmitigated severity. That the altered circumstances of modern society have afford ed to women many new sources of honourable self-support, in literature, art, and manufactures, of which they have largely a vailed themselves : That great interests have thus arisen, which it is full time should be recognised and adequately protected by the State. That the Political disqualification of women, in a country which boasts that all are equal before the law, should make the British Legislature especially anxious to improve her condition, and jealously to protect her civil and social rights. That the condition of woman, and her Idlvidual rights, have been considered, and legally protected, in the United States of America, and other countries, and with the best efiects. Wherefore your Petitioners humbly pray that your honourable House will be pleased to take into your earnest and tamediate consideration the condition of women in this country ; and also cause inquiry to be made as to the condition of women and the laws respecting them, In other countries ; and promote such legislation as, in the wisdom of your honourable House, you may deem fit to remedy the 'grievances of which your Petitioners complain.

And your Petitioners Su Generally admitted grievances are here stated with firmness and energy, and the petitioners request inquiry and investigation. but is an important and difficult one ; The subject evil cannot, and much good must arise from collecting facts and opinions with regard to the position of woman and the laws affecting her in this and other countries. As the movement proceeds from Mrs. Howitt, Mrs. Jameson, Miss Martineau, and the leading literary ladies of the day, supported by Lord Brougham, Lord Lyndhurst, Charles Dickens, and many others of the highest talent and reputation of the male sex, there cannot be a doubt that important results will arise out of the agitation . Sir Erskine Perry has gallantly taken charge of the case in the HotfSe of Commons, and has given notice of a motion for the 22nd of April. We understand it is his intention to move for a Select Commmittee, before which evidence will be received bearing on the subject ; and on the report of the committee a bill will be framed to correct or supply any deficiencies in the law as it now stands. þÿ Willmer 4 Smith's European Times.
